title: Enhancing Mars
text:
Skim through before Tuesday, no bring-to-class.
The Perseverance rover takes hundreds of pictures a day on Mars. A lot of them look murky. Today we’ll pick one and pull out the detail that’s hiding in it. The trick is that a picture is just an array of numbers, so everything we’ve learned about arrays (math on a whole array at once, masks, slicing) turns into image processing. We’ll build up the idea on tiny pictures first, then go get a real one from Mars, then work through a toolbox of techniques: contrast, color, blur, sharpen, edges.

title: Enhancing Mars
section: A picture is a grid of numbers
text:
A picture is a grid of numbers
A grayscale image is a 2D array: rows and columns of numbers, one per pixel, where 0 is black and 255 is white.
Here’s a tiny “image,” six pixels tall and eight wide:






Try things: change one of the 20s to 255. Make a second bright spot. Make the whole thing dimmer with one line (img = img / 2… what does the picture do?). Note row 0 is at the top, and row numbers grow downward.


Why 255? Each pixel’s brightness is stored in one byte. One byte is eight bits, and bits are either 0 or 1, so with eight bits available we have $2^8=256 possible combinations.

title: Enhancing Mars
text:
Color is three grids
A color image stores three numbers per pixel: how much red, how much green, how much blue. So its shape is (rows, columns, 3), and each of those three “layers” is called a channel. Here’s a tiny one, two pixels tall and three wide:






Top row: pure red, pure green, pure blue. Bottom row: red + green light makes… yellow (this is light, not paint, so the mixing rules are different from art class). All three at full is white, and equal amounts of all three is gray.
Try: change the gray pixel to [200, 100, 0]. What color do you predict? Then pull out the green channel and the blue channel the same way we pulled out red.
That last observation is worth holding on to: if the red, green, and blue channels are identical, the “color” image is really a gray image.

section: Go get a picture from Mars
text:
Go get a picture from Mars
Browse the rover’s raw images here: https://mars.nasa.gov/mars2020/multimedia/raw-images/
Scroll through a few hundred. (This is a task where your eyes are much faster than any code.) Some tips:

Filter by camera. Mastcam-Z (the rover’s main “eyes,” up on the mast) is where most of the color pictures come from. Navcam and the Hazcams are mostly black and white.
The boring-looking ones are the best candidates: murky, dark, washed out, low contrast. There’s more hiding in them. 

When you find one you like, click it, then right-click the big image and choose Copy Image Address (on an iPad: press and hold, then Copy). You’ll get a long web address ending in .jpg or .png. The version ending in _1200.jpg is plenty big.
Now in Colab, paste the toolbox below into the first cell and run it (it doesn’t do anything yet, it just defines functions), then load your picture:
url = "https://mars.nasa.gov/mars2020-raw-images/pub/ods/surface/sol/..."   # paste yours
img = load(url)

print(img.shape)
show([img], ["raw"])
Check the shape: (rows, columns, 3)? Then check whether it’s actually color:
print(np.array_equal(img[:, :, 0], img[:, :, 1]))     # is red exactly equal to green?
True means you’ve found a gray image in disguise: three identical channels. You may want to go back and pick a different one… or not, there are plenty of things to do even with gray images.

Enhancing Mars
text:
Reading a histogram
A histogram counts how many pixels have each brightness:
histogram(img)
The horizontal axis is brightness, from black on the left to white on the right. The height is how many pixels have that brightness. A dark, murky picture has most of its pixels in a narrow range on the left. A well-exposed picture spreads across most of the range.
What does yours look like? Is there anything at all out near 1?

title: Enhancing Mars
text:
Stretching
Here’s a real example from sol 2012 (October 2026): a Mastcam-Z picture of the calibration target, taken with almost no light. Its histogram is the lump on the bottom left. Every pixel is between about 0.04 and 0.14. Nothing is even remotely bright.

The fix is to stretch: take the darkest pixels we care about and make them black, take the brightest and make them white, and spread everything in between evenly. That’s a straight line:
\[
\text{new} = \frac{\text{old} - \text{lo}}{\text{hi} - \text{lo}}
\]
Check the ends: a pixel at exactly lo becomes \(0/(\text{hi}-\text{lo}) = 0\), black. A pixel at hi becomes 1, white. Halfway between becomes 0.5. Anything darker than lo or brighter than hi would land below 0 or above 1, so np.clip pins those at 0 and 1.
How do we choose lo and hi? We could use the very darkest and brightest pixels, but one stray hot pixel would wreck that. Instead, stretch uses percentiles: by default, lo is a brightness that only 1% of pixels are darker than, and hi is one that only 1% are brighter than. We sacrifice the extreme 1% at each end (they become pure black or pure white) to make the other 98% use the whole range.
s = stretch(img)
show([img, s], ["raw", "stretched"])
histogram(s)
In the example, the target comes out of the dark: rings, bolts, the little color chips along the bottom. That information was in the picture all along. It was just all squeezed into a sliver of the brightness range, too dark for us to tell apart.
Try stretch(img, 5, 95) and stretch(img, 0, 100). What changes?

title: Enhancing Mars
section: The comb: what enhancement can’t do
text:
The comb: what enhancement can’t do
Now look closely at the stretched histogram in the example. It isn’t a smooth hill. It’s a comb: spikes with empty gaps between them.
The raw image stored brightness as whole numbers from 0 to 255, and the middle 98% of its pixels used only the values 11 through 35. That’s just 25 different shades. Stretching spread those 25 shades out across the whole range… but it’s still 25 shades, the number value must still be a whole number.

title: Enhancing Mars
text:
Is an enhanced picture honest?
Stretching a picture means choosing which range of brightness to spread across the screen. It’s spiritually similar to zooming in a plot’s y-axis: set_ylim versus stretch. Neither one changes the data, but both change what a reader thinks they’re seeing.
But what color is Mars? The raw pictures come out reddish-brown. stretch_each stretches each channel separately, which usually strips that cast away and leaves things looking grayer and “cleaner.” Is that a better picture, or a less truthful one? (Mars really is red.)
The rover team’s actual answer involves the calibration target. Its gray squares are known to be gray, so if they come out tinted in a picture, the tint came from the lighting and the camera, not the target. white_balance is a correction: give it the rows and columns of a patch you know should be gray (read them off the axes of plt.imshow), and it scales the three channels until that patch is gray.
plt.imshow(img)       # find a gray square on the target; note its rows and columns
plt.show()

wb = white_balance(img, 850, 900, 420, 470)       # top, bottom, left, right: your numbers here
show([img, wb], ["raw", "white balanced"])
What does that do to the color of the ground? The target was sitting in Martian light, so “make the target gray” means “show the scene as if it were lit by Earth-like white light.”

title: Enhancing Mars
text:
The rest of the toolbox
Here’s every tool applied to one picture of the calibration target. Click to enlarge.

The tools come in two families.
One pixel at a time. stretch, gamma, invert, gray, scale_channels, remove_reds, white_balance, false_color, and threshold all compute each new pixel from that same pixel.

gamma(img, 0.5) is \(\text{new} = \text{old}^{0.5}\). Because brightness is between 0 and 1, a power less than 1 lifts dark values a lot and bright values only a little (\(0.04^{0.5} = 0.2\), but \(0.81^{0.5} = 0.9\)). Good for digging into shadows.
remove_reds multiplies the red channel by zero. On Mars, that’s a dramatic change (everything goes teal), which tells you how much of the scene’s “color” lives in the red channel.
false_color maps brightness onto a color scale, the way a thermal camera does. It can make subtle brightness differences easier to see, but the colors are invented: purple means “darker,” not “purple.”

Neighborhoods. blur, sharpen, and edges compute each new pixel from the pixel and its neighbors.

blur replaces each pixel with an average of the pixels around it (nearby ones count more). Smooths out noise, and detail with it.
sharpen is a clever trick. If blur(img) is the picture without its fine detail, then img - blur(img) is just the fine detail. Extra of that is added back: \(\text{sharpened} = \text{img} + \text{amount} \times \text{detail}\). Turn amount up to 5 and look closely: you’ll see bright halos along edges, and the noise gets “sharpened” too. More sharpening stops meaning more detail at some point.
edges asks how much each pixel differs from the pixel to its right and the pixel below it. Where the picture is smooth, neighbors are nearly equal, the differences are about zero, and the result is black. At an edge there’s a big jump, and it lights up. The two differences get combined with Pythagoras, \(\sqrt{dx^2 + dy^2}\), the same way we’d combine an east-west and a north-south distance. One subtraction finds the outline of every rock!

title: Pandas
text:
A test rig logging 100 readings per second produces 360,000 rows an hour. We can technically store that hour of data in a spreadsheet and open it with Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets, but prepare for a headache: scrolling through the data set is clumsy, creating figures will be laggy, and writing math equations will involve cryptic things like =PI()*AL2… what is AL2?!
Pandas is a Python package that excels (hehe) at dealing with large datasets. Rather than having an interface that constantly displays the data, the data is stored in a variable name and accessed by column name — “temperature_C” instead of “AL2”. There are ways to filter and sort the data and calculate the statistics of it, and the data can be analyzed using Python scripts instead of scrolling around a spreadsheet, creating columns, etc.

title: Pandas
section: When spreadsheets are no longer useful
text:
When spreadsheets are no longer useful
Excel has its role in an engineer’s toolbox: for small tables where it is possible to inspect the entire dataset with just a bit of scrolling, it is great. If you need to do a little bit of math on that data, e.g. adding two columns together, it is great — easy to check your work, and you can quickly look over the results.
It is not so great whenever you have 400,000 rows and 24 columns — a very reasonable situation if a collection of sensors is harvesting data several times per second. Then imagine an ensuing analysis, maybe something delivered to you by a colleague: cell Y2 is referenced by A2, but you don’t know what is in Y2, so you scroll over. The number in Y2 looks suspicious so you want to check it with a “quick” calculation. Right-click, create a new column, start creating a formula, scroll around to find the cells you need in the formula and click them, get yelled at by Microsoft because there is a problem with the equation, fix it, propagate it down through all 400,000 rows.
And then imagine having to do the same thing with every spreadsheet that is produced by your testing process… each time manually creating columns, scrolling all over the spreadsheet to do so, typing the same equation into each spreadsheet. The point is: yes, one can do this, but there is a better way.

title: Pandas
text:
Pandas and the DataFrame
Pandas is a Python package (typically imported with import pandas as pd) designed to handle large datasets. Its core object is the DataFrame: a table (basically a spreadsheet) stored under one variable name (here df):
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("motor_test_log.csv")
df.head()
head() is a useful initial check — make sure the data looks like it should. It prints the column names and first few rows of data. Columns are labeled by name, not a cryptic AL2:
df["temp_C"]            # one column is called temp_C
df["temp_C"].mean()
df["temp_C"].max()
df.describe()           # summary statistics for every numeric column at once

title: Pandas
text:
Filter, summarize, reduce
Filtering is like masking:
hot = df[df["temp_C"] > 80]      # a new DataFrame: only the too-hot rows
len(hot)                          # how many rows are there?
hot["rpm"].mean()                 # within the hot DataFrame, what was the average rpm?
Read the inner part first: df["temp_C"] > 80 produces 60,000 True/False values; wrapping it in df[...] keeps the rows that are True. Grouping let’s you examine the data “broken down by…”:
df.groupby("test_phase")["temp_C"].mean()   # average temp in each phase of the test
Importantly, these commands are part of a Python script — you can run the same script for each of your files and get “the average temp in each phase of the test” (or whatever).

Having many tools in your toolbox
Excel has its place, and knowing when to use it vs. when to use Pandas is wisdom you will develop. I use Excel when I want to actually see the data with a reasonable amount of scrolling. E.g., at the end of the semester I open the gradebook in Excel and have a look around, maybe add a column with a calculation and see what happens or something.
But if I have a large dataset (more than a few hundred rows) and want to do some sort of analysis on it, its time for Pandas. Especially if I might need to do that analysis on several different datasets — one Pandas script can be applied to all the files, without clumsily scrolling through each one.

title: A loop that remembers — simulating a falling ball
text:
Last week we used for loops to compare designs: five rotor diameters, and eleven blade designs, one per v_best value. The order didn’t matter: we could have swept the diameters backwards, or shuffled them, and every answer would have come out the same. The passes through the loop were independent.
This week we add one wrinkle: what if each pass needs to know what the last pass worked out? Last week: the loop evaluated a formula many times; today: the loop builds an answer that has no formula. If you’ve ever heard someone say the computer is simulating a result, this is it!

title: A loop that remembers — simulating a falling ball
section: A rule instead of a formula
text:
A rule instead of a formula
In several places on this webpage, we’ve been using
\[
t = \sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}
\]
to describe how long a dropped object takes to fall. That is a “formula”, but it is very idealized, notably neglecting drag. Many times in engineering, we don’t have an explicit formula that connects an input to an output, but we do have a rule that we can use computationally to get an approximation of the connection.
Let’s keep thinking about the drop time, and we will build up to something more complex by Thursday. Suppose I tell you a ball is 10 m high and, at that moment, falling at 3 m/s. If we measure \(y\) upward from the ground, then falling means \(v = -3\) m/s. Where is it one tenth of a second from now? You might note
\[
\Delta y = (-3\text{ m/s})(0.1\text{ s}) = -0.3\text{ m}
\]
— three tenths of a meter lower than it started — and that would be pretty close, although the ball does speed up during that interval (because gravity manifests as an acceleration). We could write these rules generally as
\[
\begin{align*}
y_{\text{new}} &= y + v\,\Delta t \\
v_{\text{new}} &= v + a\,\Delta t
\end{align*}
\]
The first of these equations says: your new position is your old position plus however far you traveled. The second says the same thing about speed: your new velocity is your old velocity plus however much gravity changed it. If we wanted to predict how far you’ve moved, we could calculate these two things over and over again, keeping track of the position \(y\) and velocity \(v\) after every “time step” \(\Delta t\). Do it a few hundred times and you can trace the trajectory of a falling object.






Important



Notice the speed changes each time we do the calculation, and so the displacement \(y_\text{new}-y\) will change as well (assuming the same \(\Delta t\)).








Tip



Pay attention to signs! If \(y\) is measured upward from the ground, and then the object falls with gravity, the acceleration \(a = -9.81\) m/s² is negative! The velocity \(v\) will also be negative. More important than memorizing conventions is paying attention to the physics and making sure it matches with your intuition.

title: A loop that remembers — simulating a falling ball
text:
Keeping track
Those two rules are each an accumulator: y = y + something, v = v + something — same idea as total = total + x. The only difference is that now there are two of them and they rely on each other.
We’ll keep track of the values of these two things in NumPy arrays, and we’ll need to read element i in order to write element i+1. Here is how we build it:








With this scheme, the first time step forward leaves us at the original value of \(y\). This isn’t a bug — our initial value of \(v\) is zero, and in this discrete approximation of real physical behavior, that causes \(y\) to be the same in its first two values.
A few notes:
There are n_steps + 1 slots for n_steps steps. Taking 30 steps means starting in one state, then moving to 30 new states. Off-by-one errors are common!
Element zero is the initial condition. y[0] = 10.0 is not a calculation, it’s an input: we say that it starts at a height of 10.
The loop reads i and writes i+1. This can’t be done with a NumPy array operation, no matter how clever. y[i+1] needs v[i], which needed v[i-1]… all the way back to the beginning. NumPy can do a million multiplications at once because none are dependent on each other. Here, the dominoes have to fall in order.

title: A loop that remembers — simulating a falling ball
text:
Let’s plot it






Does this match expectation? The speed should increase with time, as gravity causes an acceleration. This will manifest as a curve that starts flat and then steepens.
What might be unexpected: the object punches through \(y=0\) and ends up thirty-two meters underground.






ImportantThe model knows only what you told it



Nowhere in that loop did we mention that the ground exists, or that balls stop at it. We told the program one thing — gravity pulls down.
A simulation is a small set of rules we chose… the computer does exactly what we tell it to do. If we don’t tell it about the ground, it doesn’t do anything about the ground!

title: A loop that remembers — simulating a falling ball
text:
Is any of this right?
A verification question! We have been assuming no air resistance — in such a case there is a formula we can check against:
\[y = h_0 - \tfrac{1}{2} g t^2\]
At \(t = 1.0\) s from 10 m, that’s \(10 - 0.5(9.81)(1) = 5.095\) m. Let’s see what our stepper says, at a few different step sizes.






Two things to note:
Smaller steps, smaller error. At dt = 0.5 we’re off by 2.45 m, terrible; at dt = 0.01 we’re off by 5 cm. The price for taking smaller steps is taking more steps, but the computer doesn’t mind.
But the velocity is exactly right at every step size. The velocity comes out to \(-9.810\) in every row… gravity is constant, so v = v - g*dt isn’t an approximation at all; it’s exact. Velocity is not constant during a step, though, and y = y + v*dt pretends it is: we use the speed from the start of the step for the whole step, so we under-count the distance fallen and our ball sits a little too high.
So this new method works, but why bother when the formula is exact and easier to program? Because the formula only exists for the idealized problem. The equation \(y = h_0 - \frac12 g t^2\) is true because the acceleration is constant — if the acceleration depends on anything, the simple formula is no longer applicable. But… the loop method doesn’t even notice! Just tell your code the new value for a and it is ready to go!
Why would it change? Most notably: air resistance — air pushes back harder the faster you go, so the acceleration depends on the velocity… but the velocity depends on the acceleration… which depends on the velocity. For our time-stepper it’s one extra line, inside the body we already wrote.

title: A loop that remembers — simulating a falling ball
text:
Challenge
Which angle throws the ball farthest?
Now throw the ball forward and up, at an angle \(\theta\) above the ground. The ball moves in two directions at once, so it needs a position and a velocity in each: \(x\) and \(y\), \(v_x\) and \(v_y\). The rules are the same ones as before, written out once for each direction:
\[
\begin{align*}
x_{\text{new}} &= x + v_x\,\Delta t & y_{\text{new}} &= y + v_y\,\Delta t \\
v_{x,\text{new}} &= v_x + a_x\,\Delta t & v_{y,\text{new}} &= v_y + a_y\,\Delta t
\end{align*}
\]
Vertically nothing has changed: \(a_y = -g\). If we are ignoring drag, there is no acceleration in the \(x\)-direction: \(a_x=0\).
Throwing at speed \(v_0\) and angle \(\theta\) splits the throw into a sideways part and an upward part:
\[
v_{x} = v_0 \cos\theta, \qquad v_{y} = v_0 \sin\theta \qquad \text{(at the start)}
\]


As in HW 2, NumPy’s cos and sin want radians. np.radians converts degree measurements to radians, or you can start thinking in radians!

Build it. Throw from the ground at 10 m/s and 30°. Plot the path of the ball — y against x. Where does it land?
Check it against physics. A 30° throw and a 60° throw should land in the same place (assuming no drag). Do yours? How close is “the same”?
Sweep it. Put your throw inside a function, landing_distance(angle), that returns where the ball lands. Then run it for every angle from 5° to 85°, keep the answers in a pre-allocated array, and use argmax to find the best angle. Plot distance against angle.
Question the famous answer. Everything so far launched from the ground. Launch from hand height, 1.5 m — then from the top of a 10 m building. Does the best angle stay the same?





A loop inside a loop is called a nested loop. The inner one always runs to completion before the outer one takes its next step.

title: Packages and arrays
text:
Week 3 ended with a question: we wanted to know which wind speed produced the most power, and the only tool we had available was calling the function over and over by hand.
Let’s give it a bit more narrative: let’s suppose we are trying to estimate the amount of energy that would be produced by our turbine, based on wind speed data taken every hour. Calling your function 24 times by hand is… fine. But there is a better approach (and there will be problems in our future that necessitate calling a function 1000 times, so we’ll soon require a better approach).
This lesson introduces two ideas that will help us solve this problem: packages (code other people already wrote for you) and arrays (many numbers stored under one variable name). By the end, those 24 function calls become one line.

title: Packages and arrays
text:
Think First
Recall

Week 3: why did I recommend the efficiency curve \(C_p(v)\) be its own function, instead of burying it inside the power function?
Week 3: you hunted for the best wind speed by re-running the code. How many runs did you do before it got old?

Look Ahead

What if we had wind speed values measured every minute throughout the day (1440 pieces of data). Can we call the power function 1440 times without having to type 1440 lines?
If a program hands back 1440 answers, how do you check that they’re right without reading all 1440?

title: Packages and arrays
section: Packages: code other people already wrote
text:
Packages: code other people already wrote
Almost nothing you compute as an engineer will be built from scratch. Someone has already written, tested, and optimized code for square roots, statistics, curve fits, plotting, and file reading — and they’ve collected that code into a package you can import and use.
The big one for us is NumPy, short for numerical python, which includes pretty much all of the basic mathematical functions used by engineers. Mathematical operations like \(\sqrt{x}\) and \(\exp{(x)}\) are useful:








I originally planned to hold-off on packages until later, but many of you were importing NumPy to get np.pi on Thursday. This nudged me towards introducing this now!
What did we do here? Step 1 is to import the package. It is typical that the very first line of your code is import numpy as np. This loads the package so that we can use the tools within it, and the as np part gives it a shorter nickname so that we can write np.sqrt instead of numpy.sqrt. (Everyone uses np, so let’s copy that convention.)
When it comes to calling the functions within the NumPy package: yes, the np. prefix is mandatory. It tells the program to call the function from the NumPy package, not from Python itself. “Base” Python does not have a built-in function called sqrt, we have to look within the NumPy package for its np.sqrt function.


There are technically ways to circumvent the np. prefix, but they are discouraged.






TipThink



The np.sqrt function has been verified by millions of users over thirty years and it is far more trustworthy than anything you or an LLM will write this semester. While np.sqrt is rock-solid, you are still responsible for using it in the right place, with the right data, etc. That is, you’ll still need to verify you are using it in the correct way.

title: Packages and arrays
section: Lists: several numbers under one name
text:
Lists: several numbers under one name
The biggest thing NumPy gets us is the ability to do math on many numbers at once. In (base) Python we can create a list of values by putting the numbers inside square brackets, separated by commas






One thing that is true with both Python lists and NumPy arrays (which we are about to introduce): they are labeled/“indexed” starting with zero. “The first” number in the list above can be retrieved using speeds[0], and so we might say speeds[4] is the fifth element.


Thoughtful engineers who use Python a lot will call these the “zeroth” elements and “fourth” elements, or “index zero” and “index four”, but it takes a mental shift to be comfortable looking at a list of numbers and then use those names.
By the way: MATLAB counts from 1. I teach in both languages and get tripped up!

title: Packages and arrays
text:
Lists don’t do math
A reasonable expectation: if speeds holds three numbers, then 2*speeds will double the values of those three numbers. Let’s find out.






Errr… it tacked-on another copy of the list? Now we have a list with six values (and no error or warning). Cubing fails too






… but at least it gives us an error message. The moral of this story: engineers use programming to do math, and “base” Python is not ready to handle the type of math we need to do. We need to bring in another tool, or package of tools, to do engineering work. NumPy!

title: Packages and arrays
text:
The NumPy array
A subtle shift in language: NumPy works with arrays, and those arrays are going to be able to do the math we hoped Python lists would do:






Technically we build an array using a Python list: np.array(...) is a function that takes as its input a list, here [4.5, 6.2, 7.8, ...]. The function turns that input into a NumPy array, and importantly, arrays will do arithmetic elementwise — the operation happens to every value at once, and you get an array of results back. If our NumPy array has eight elements and we use np.sqrt on it, we are going to get an output with eight elements.
It is hard to overstate the importance of this. When you go to do an engineering analysis, you might have a huge collection of numbers. You can store that whole list as a NumPy array with a single variable name, speeds. Then you can cube every number in that list with speeds**3. With just a couple more operations (which NumPy has available as built-in functions), you can compute the total amount of kinetic energy passing through your wind turbine in a day. You get to deal with a single variable speeds instead of individually process every value within the list!

title: Packages and arrays
section: Your week-3 function already works on arrays
text:
Your week-3 function already works on arrays
Here are examples of where you might have landed with the turbine functions from week 3. (Yours may differ in argument order, etc., and that’s fine). Without adjusting anything we can use a NumPy array as an input and will get an array of output values.






We wanted to quickly calculate the power from eight wind speeds, created a NumPy array called speeds that had eight numbers in it, and passed that into our functions to get eight values of power.
We’ll have to be a little bit more careful when the functions get more complicated — e.g., arrays are fussy if you use them with an if statement — but this is really powerful!

title: Packages and arrays
section: Reductions: turning many numbers back into one
text:
Reductions: turning many numbers back into one
An array of 8 powers is progress, but nobody wants to read 8 numbers, let alone 24, and definitely not the 60,000 we’ll meet in week 7. What we want are the handful of numbers that answer the question. Those come from reductions — operations that take a whole array and return one value. Let’s grab the code from above and add a little bit more:






Appending sum, max, min, mean to the end of a NumPy array does what you’d expect them to: sum the values (to a single number), report the maximum value, report the minimum value, and report the mean (average) value. argmax is some new vocabulary: it returns the index where the biggest value occurs. So power.max() tells you what the best hour produced and power.argmax() tells you which hour it was.






ImportantA tricky trace that you’ll get used to



Hopefully I’m not throwing too much at you but: we saw above that speeds[0] gives us the zeroth number within the array of speeds; speeds[4] gives us the “fourth” number in the array. power.argmax() will give us the index where the maximum value of power occurs, and so speeds[power.argmax()] will tell us the speed at which the maximum value of power occurs! It may seem like a tangled mess right now, but with a bit more experience the logic will become intuitive.





Notice we no longer have to inspect the outputs to figure out which is the biggest number, there is a function that does it for us!

title: Packages and arrays
section: A good habit: check the extremes
text:
A good habit: check the extremes
A problem with tools like .sum: you aren’t checking on every value, so what if there is a bad one?
Weather data conventionally marks missing values with an absurd placeholder like -999, e.g. if the sensor is iced-over or the electronics have a hiccup. Computers do exactly what you tell them to do:






The sum comes back as 2.8e+13 — a number with no error message or warning. It has no minus sign, it didn’t crash, and a tired engineer copies it into a report. It is 28 trillion kilowatt-hours: about 28,000 TWh, which is very nearly a full year of the entire world’s electricity production. I don’t think one turbine did this in six hours!






Important



Look at the extremes before you trust the sum. max() and min() are one line each and they’ll be a sanity check when your data sets are too large to look through in detail.

Is the maximum physically possible? Add the power.max() to the code above: huge.
Is the minimum physically possible? A negative power means the turbine is consuming electricity from the wind.
Then argmax or argmin tells you exactly which reading to go look at.

title: Packages and arrays
text:
Seeing it: a first plot
The second most important package in MCEN 1030 is Matplotlib… I think so-named because it stole a lot of plotting conventions from MATLAB. We’ll dive-in to plotting more seriously in a couple weeks, but let’s go ahead and introduce the basic functionality now — it will help us to verify that our data is reasonable.
Some of you went ahead and plotted \(C_p(v) = 0.45[1 - ((v-11)/8)^2]\) last week (using Desmos or something like that) — that’s great! Let’s look at it within Python, and we’ll need to do another import with another nickname:






There’s a couple new functions in here: - np.arange(0, 20.5, 0.5) created an array of wind speeds starting at 0 and taking steps of 0.5 m/s up to (but not including) 20.5 (so it stops at 20.0). In total: 41 values of wind speed stored in an array called v. - We’ve seen this before, but quick reminder: cp(v) evaluated all 41 wind speeds at once. - plt.plot(v, cp(v)) creates a plot where the x-values are the numbers in v and the y-values are the numbers calculated by cp(v).
Concerningly, the curve goes below zero on the left side at \(v = 3\) m/s, and on the right side at \(v = 19\). That is: below 3 m/s the formula reports a negative efficiency, which would mean the turbine generating negative power in a light breeze. That is not physically meaningful, it’s an example of extrapolating an equation outside its meaningful range. We should be asking what should happen at 2 m/s — something is wrong with the equation!

(1) Predict the output of each of these two lines.
print(2 * [1, 2, 3])
print(2 * np.array([1, 2, 3]))
(2) Here are Boulder’s daily highs (°F) for one week in early September:
[84, 88, 91, 95, 39, 87, 190]
No computer. Predict what temps.max(), temps.argmax(), and temps.mean() would return.

title: Packages and arrays
text:
In-class work
We’re going to revisit the wind turbine, using NumPy arrays in our functions from last week and one new trick: boolean masking.


A “boolean” is a very fancy name for a True/False value. “Masking” is when we cover-up things associated with False values and only work with the things associated with True values.
Here’s a quick example. Before you run it: what do you think the first print statement is going to do? What about the second print statement? Are these going to produce results that are the same length?






This is a boolean mask. A comparison on a whole array doesn’t give you one True or False back, it gives you an array of them — True/False is judged for every item in the array. And then indexing the array with an array of True/False keeps only the positions marked True.






Caution



Try each of these in Colab, predicting first.



Recompute the day’s energy with the bad reading masked out: turbine_power(speeds[speeds >= 0]).sum(). Compare it to the number the reading’s −999 demo produced.
Check whether masking silently dropped something: len(speeds) before, len(speeds[speeds >= 0]) after.
Combine two conditions with & (not and — that one doesn’t work elementwise): mask a new array of wind speeds down to only the ones inside the turbine’s valid operating range from the reading’s \(C_p\) plot, 3 <= v <= 19. Something like mask = (v >= 3) & (v <= 19).
For the curious: try speeds[speeds >= 0 and speeds <= 19] instead of using &. Read the error.
Try the same trick on the Boulder temperatures from the bring-to-class item: temps[temps < 150]. Compute .mean() before and after. How much does one bad reading move the average?



In Python, the “length” of a list or array is how many elements it contains. In Python, the length of an array x is len(x).






Important



Masking is fast and it is quiet — you might accidentally drop information you did not intend to, and it won’t alert you! A quick way to check how many terms you’ve dropped is to measure the length with and without the mask using len(...).

title: Packages and arrays
section: Challenge: which hours are most significant?
text:
Challenge: which hours are most significant?
Here’s a full 24-hour day for the same turbine, measuring wind speed every hour. (As is usually the case around here: calmer winds overnight and speeds build through the afternoon. Then I’ve added a sensor glitch and one gust past the model’s valid range of 3–19 m/s.)








A trick: mask is an array of True/False, and Python treats True as 1 and False as 0. So mask.sum() counts how many were True.

Using speeds[mask], compute the total power for the valid speeds only, in kWh. (I guess we’ll claim that when the system is overspeeding, we’ll stop it, and when it is too low it is just producing zero energy.)
What fraction of that total came from the single best hour? (power.max() / power.sum())
What fraction came from the top three hours combined? You’ll need a new function for this: np.sort(array) returns the values sorted smallest to largest, so the biggest three are the last three: np.sort(power)[-3:]. Look up np.sort (or ask your favorite LLM to explain it), predict what [-3:] does to a sorted array before you run it, then compute the top-3 share of the day’s total.





We’re secretly doing a bit of Calculus here: “total power” will just be the sum of the power values every hour. (There’s an extra multiplicative factor involved but the total power will be proportional to our result.)

title: Reading code and conditional statements
text: Tuesday we ran code and thought about the results, today we are going to focus on how read and understand the code without needing to run it. Included is an example of the spec → prompt → annotate → verify process. Then we go through conditional statements, which bring us to the interesting and sometimes-confusing world of branching logic: if something is True, do this, but if False, do something else.

title: Reading code and conditional statements
text:

title: Reading code and conditional statements
text:
The reading vocabulary
You already know enough Python to read most short engineering scripts. Here’s a beginning inventory:


Truthfully, much of what I code is handling arithmetic — nothing fancy at all. Take these numbers, square them and multiply by this constant, and plot the result. You don’t know plotting yet, but you are quickly learning to understand how math is represented in code.



You see
It means

store 5 under the name x (“x is assigned 5”)


print(x)

power, division

title: Reading code and conditional statements
section: Tracing: running code in your head
text:
Tracing: running code in your head
To trace a program, be the computer: go top to bottom, one line at a time, keeping a little table of every variable’s current value. (Run the code after your trace to confirm your suspicions.)












NoteClick to see the trace





After line 1: a = 2, with b and c not yet defined. After line 2: a = 2, b = 5. After line 3: a = 20, b = 5. After line 4: c = 25.



Tracing is slow and that’s fine — it’s a verification strategy you’ll only deploy on the sections you aren’t sure about

title: Reading code and conditional statements
text:
Annotation
When an AI hands you code, you will annotate it. That’s not the same as reading the comments the AI already left, it means writing, in your own words, what every line or logical block does and why it’s there. Producing that explanation yourself, not just reading someone else’s, is what actually proves you understand the code.






Important



Rule 1: A line you can’t annotate is a line you do not understand.
Rule 2: Annotate the why, not just the what. # convert to liters is better than # multiply by 1000. (The latter is probably a repeat of the code!)

title: Reading code and conditional statements
text:
One full lap: the 3D-printer problem
The problem: How much filament will it take to 3D-print this part?
Step 1 — Specification. Inputs — part volume (cm³), infill fraction (0–1), filament diameter (mm). Output — filament length needed, in meters. Assumptions — filament is drawn out as a solid cylinder, no waste from priming or purge lines, infill fraction distributed uniformly. Edge cases — zero diameter will raise a division-by-zero error rather than silently returning a bad result.


The slicer is the software that turns a 3D model into printing instructions. The infill fraction is the fraction of a part’s interior that is plastic — if its value is, say, 0.20, the interior of an apparently solid object is a lattice that is 20% plastic and 80% air.
Step 2 — The prompt. The spec practically is the prompt:

Write a Python script that computes the length of filament needed to 3D-print a part. Inputs: part volume in cubic centimeters, infill fraction (0 to 1), and filament diameter in millimeters. Output the filament length in meters including units. Comment each step, including tracking the units/unit conversions along the way.

Step 3 — Annotate what comes back. Suppose the AI returns:






Some initial good news: the code runs without any error messages, and every line is commented and makes sense. We’ve annotated three lines… these are worth checking: are the conversions and equations correct? They are chances for a silent error that would deliver an incorrect output!


You don’t necessarily need to comment every line, especially if the variable names are intuitive. You also might be able to comment on an entire block at once, or if there are repeated steps just describe the first one, or … . Just make sure your code+comments is understandable!
Step 4 — Verify. Hand estimate: the printed volume is \(45 \times 0.20 = 9\) cm³ = 9,000 mm³. The filament’s cross-section is roughly \(\pi (0.875)^2 \approx 2.4\) mm². So the required length is \(\approx 9{,}000 / 2.4 \approx 3{,}750\) mm \(\approx 3.75\) m. We were careful with units here, good. Edge case: set diameter = 0 and predict what happens before running.


You might ask: why did we write a program, and then calculate it by hand anyway? It’s good to have the confirmation — we might not trust the AI, and we might not trust our algebra, but if they agree we can feel better about both. But more importantly: we will get into functions next week, where we write code that can accept different input values, and maybe we use that function 1000 times on a project. With functions, we’ll check on one or two cases by hand, and if it’s good we can feel OK about using that function for the other 998 cases.

When the AI gets it plausibly wrong
The AI might return something like
volume_filled_mm3 = volume_filled_cm3 * 100    # convert cm^3 to mm^3
(E.g., centimeters to meters is a factor of 100… maybe it sees cm and conversion and assumes we are going that way.) It runs and reports a filament length of 0.37 m — maybe believable, but wrong by a factor of ten.

title: Reading code and conditional statements
text:
One more thing: if/elif/else
Code tracing through algebra, checking unit conversions and area equations, etc., is important but kind of boring. Let’s go ahead and introduce conditional statements in this reading: they lead to branching… the code takes different paths depending on whether a condition is True or False.

Conditions
Conditions are expressions that evaluate to either True or False. Very useful in coding, e.g. if we are doing a fluid mechanics calculation, the pressure-drop equation we use depends on whether the flow is laminar or turbulent. Our code might check “is the flow turbulent?” If False, it will proceed with the laminar equation; if True, it will proceed with the turbulent equation.
Here are examples of all six basic conditions:



Condition
Meaning




x == 5
“x is equal to 5”


b!=3
“b is not equal to 3”


a>3
“a is greater than 3”


a>=2
“a is greater than or equal to 2”


c<-99
“c is less than negative 99”


c<=8
“c is less than or equal to 8”





The double equals == is the “conditional equals”, the single equals = is the “assignment equals”. 5=3 will get you an error, but 5==3 will be interpreted as False, and the program will keep running no problem.
These conditions evaluate as either True or False:






Conditional statements can also be combined, and in Python it is really nice: we get to use the words and and or. Statements with and or or can still be evaluated as True or False


MATLAB, Java, C, C++, and others use && and || for “and” and “or”… not too bad, but not as readable as and and or!






and we can make it pretty complicated by combining these expressions!








if statements
These are very readable, so let’s just dive in with a basic example:






This is an if statement. If the condition described after the if is True, Python executes the code inside the block that follows; if it is False, it skips it.


In Python, a block is a collection of lines with the same amount of indent level. Python is a unique language in that it defines its blocks based on the indent — in other languages we enclose blocks in braces {} or maybe we introduce a block with an if and end it explicitly with a line that just says end. Many folks enjoy Python because it is uncluttered.






Warning



Python’s indented blocks are very nice, the code looks very clean, but you have to be accurate with your spacing. This is fine:






and this is fine






but this will break








Be alert for rogue spaces!


if/else statements
This is pretty intuitive as well:






This is an if/else statement: it checks the condition after the if and, if it’s true, it executes the code within the if block but not the code within the else block. If the condition after the if is false it skips the code within the if block and executes the code within the else block.


if/elif/else statements
A third structure:


In Python, elif is “else if”.






This is an if/else if/else statement: it checks the condition after the if and, if it is True, it executes the if block then skips the elif and else blocks. If the condition after the if is False, it checks the condition after the elif, and if that is True, it executes the elif block and skips the else block. If both the if and elif conditions are False, it executes the code within the else block.
I feel like explaining that in a paragraph might have been more confusing than just reading the code!






Important



You can add more than one elif. The conditions are always checked from top to bottom, and the first one that evaluates as True is the only part of the structure that is actually executed by Python.
It is not mandatory to have an else statement. If none of the if/elif conditions are True and there is no else, it is effectively the same as just skipping the whole block. Sometimes that is desired!




Nested conditional statements
By using two levels of indentation, we can create nested conditional statements. Try to understand the following…












Tip



If the if statement is false, we move on to the elif. If the elif statement is True, we execute its block. Within there, we’ve got another if to consider.


The hardest trace on this page!

Below is an AI-generated script with three planted flaws: one syntax error (won’t run), one loud error (runs, obviously wrong), and one silent error (runs, plausibly wrong). On paper: annotate every line, name all three flaws, trace the if statement and say whether its warning prints, and state what the correct filament length should be. Don’t run it first, you are here to learn!
import math

diameter     = 1.75    # filament diameter, mm
part_volume  = 45      # part volume, cm^3
infill       = 0.20    # fraction of volume actually printed
spool_volume = 285     # cm^3 of plastic on a standard 1 kg spool

volume_filled = part_volume * infill      # cm^3 of plastic actually extruded
volume_mm3    = volume_filled * 1000      # convert cm^3 to mm^3
area          = math.pi * diameter ** 2   # cross-sectional area of filament, mm^2
length_mm     = area / volume_mm3         # mm of filament needed
length_m      = length_mm / 1000          # convert mm to m

if volume_filled > spool_volume:
    print("warning: volume larger than standard spool size")

print("Filament needed:", length_m "m")





We’re building a collection of error messages. In class on Tuesday we encountered NameError (used a variable name Python has never seen before), SyntaxError (the code is not valid Python — it can’t run), and TypeError (e.g., we tried to do math with data that was interpreted as text: in 5+“15”, the 15 is text). Setting diameter = 0 back in Step 4 gives a ZeroDivisionError (you asked Python to divide by zero). When we had inconsistent indentation in the if block, we got an IndentationError.

title: What does an LLM actually do?
text: You will use AI consistently in this course and you might have some experience already. (If not, don’t worry!) Let’s spend one lesson on what’s it’s actually doing.

title: What does an LLM actually do?
text:
Think First
Recall

Your phone’s keyboard suggests the next word as you type. How do you think it decides what to suggest?
Have you ever confidently “remembered” something that turned out to be wrong?

Look Ahead

If two students give an AI the exact same prompt, will they get the exact same code back?
Why might an AI be better at writing code than at doing arithmetic?
crumbs: What does an LLM actually do?

title: What does an LLM actually do?
text:
The short version
A large language model (LLM) does one thing:

Given some text, predict a plausible next small chunk of text.

That’s it. Everything else — the code-writing, the explanations, the apparent reasoning — emerges from doing that one thing extremely well, at enormous scale.


The “small chunks” are called tokens — usually a word or piece of a word. thermal might be one token; thermodynamics might be three. (Different than the tokens involved in our standards-based grading scheme!)
The model learned to do this by, in effect, reading a colossal amount of text — books, articles, documentation, and importantly for us, billions of lines of code — and adjusting billions (perhaps trillions) of internal numerical knobs until its “next-chunk” predictions got very good. This is what we mean when we talk about a new LLM “model” — there are more parameters (knobs) and updated tunings of those knobs that do a better job of creating accurate/plausible bodies of text.
crumbs: What does an LLM actually do?

title: What does an LLM actually do?
text:
Three consequences
Everything strange about LLM behavior falls out of that mechanism.

1. Its answers are plausible, but might not be true
The model produces text that is statistically likely to follow your prompt — the text sounds like what the correct answer might sound like. It is not reasoning based on physics, it has read a bunch of text written by humans who reasoned based on physics. Then it realized, statistically, that whenever those humans mention “physics”, “black holes”, and “singularity”, it is probably appropriate to use the word “Hawking”, and a likely word after that is “radiation”.


One concerning thing about LLMs is that they are increasingly being trained on text generated by LLMs — so much internet content is generated by LLMs that the LLMs are reinforcing their own tendencies and possibly that will lead to quality degrading over generations.
Usually, the most plausible continuation of an engineering question is the correct answer, which is why these tools are often useful. But when the model doesn’t “know,” it does not stop and say so. It keeps generating plausible text — a medical treatment suggestion that doesn’t apply to the situation (dangerous!), a citation to a paper that doesn’t exist, a recipe with a cup of vanilla instead of a teaspoon. This is often called a hallucination, and the dangerous part is that the LLM can be just as confident about a hallucination as it is about real information.






Important



There is no tone difference between an LLM being right and an LLM being wrong. Verify!




2. Same prompt, different answers
Prediction produces a menu of plausible next chunks, each with a probability. By design, the model doesn’t always pick the single most likely one. A bit of controlled randomness in the choice makes output more varied and, usually, better. Run the same prompt twice and the choices fork somewhere, and once forked, the two continuations keep diverging.


LLMs with a higher “temperature” value (not the physical temperature) are more likely to choose a token with a lower probability. An LLM with zero temperature chooses the most probable token every time — for a given prompt, it creates the same output every time.
This is why, on Thursday, 15 tables prompting for the same task will produce 15 different programs — different variable names, different structures, sometimes different algorithms, occasionally different answers. Thinking about that is an important aspect of this class!


3. A good specification tames the LLM
A prompt is the text you supply to the LLM, maybe a question. An effective prompt is thoughtful… it’s not like a Google search where you just say some relevant words (“lyrics steely dan”) and then you, yourself, look through the results to find what you are looking for. You should be supplying instructions, relevant context, and constraints.


Does anyone else find it annoying that Google’s first result is now AI? Whenever I don’t know exactly what I am looking for, being able to scan the first few results is usually what it takes to figure it out; and whenever I do know what I am looking for, I am not interested in Gemini’s mediocre summary!
“Build me a diet plan” is too general to be immediately useful… are you trying to lose weight? Gain weight? Gain muscle? Add more fiber? Eliminate carbs? Allergic to nuts? The LLM will probably follow up with questions like that, and you’ll end up somewhere good, but sometimes it might make assumptions for you that you have to spend time undoing. (“Yuck, it wants me to eat fish three times a week!”)
Rather than arguing with the LLM for 15 minutes, wasting a bunch of water and electricity in the process, you should be thoughtful about your specifications.


The context window is the cap on how much of that text the model can “see” at once — your current prompt, along with (at least some of) your previous questions in the same conversation, any files you’ve included. And maybe you’ve given the LLM some baseline instructions that are automatically applied to all conversations. There is a limit on how much of that information can be included in a given text-generation step, and even if it were all included, the more context it has, the greater chance of getting confused! I suspect part of the model development that is happening is about doing a better job understanding what in the context window is most relevant to your current prompt.

title: What does an LLM actually do?
section: Why is it so good at code, anyway?
text:
Why is it so good at code, anyway?
The biggest reason: the training data included billions of lines of code, much of it from working programs, and a lot of solid documentation from the code creators themselves ( find_peaks). So there is a strong statistical signal that these are very relevant words for this task.
But furthermore: code is checkable. Compare

“You can’t fix every problem, so just focus on doing good work in your own corner of it.”

with

“It is not our part to master all the tides of the world, but to do what is in us for the succour of those years wherein we are set, uprooting the evil in the fields that we know, so that those who live after may have clean earth to till.”

How can you judge that the first one is “wrong”? Based on our understanding of how LLMs work, every new word/token in that line is a completely reasonable continuation of the sentence. The second one, by Tolkien, is better, but not “more correct”.
Meanwhile: if code doesn’t run, something is wrong, and we further will get an output from code that can possibly be confirmed/validated against known results. Modern LLMs are able to run code on the cloud to confirm they perform as intended, and they are increasingly willing to compare against test cases for you: if you need some code to find the area under a curve, an LLM might write it, run it, and compare against the known area under \(y=x\) from 0 to 1. Basically, the LLMs are doing their own small verification. That probably isn’t sufficient to confirm that the code does what it is supposed to, but it is necessary that the code works for at least that basic problem.
We will do our own audit and verification of the code: read through it to make sure it follows a logic we agree with, and test its output in several ways. We may need to iterate — the AI gives us code that seems like it is 90% of the way to succeeding at the job, but there is an error, and so we need to work with the AI to revise. Unlike prose, we can identify specifics about what is wrong and eventually arrive at something that is verified correct.


Meanwhile: LLMs are historically mediocre at arithmetic — predicting a text representation of numbers in a calculation is not the same as calculating.

title: What does an LLM actually do?
section: The stance on LLMs in this course
text:
The stance on LLMs in this course
No doubt, LLMs are tools that can augment your abilities. A few years ago I might have manually combined 40 spreadsheets into one (which maybe would have taken an hour, but was annoying), or I might have written code to do that for me (which probably would have taken four hours to figure out… should have just done it manually arggg). Now I can ask an LLM to give me the Python code to do it, and the project is done in 5 minutes.
I have become more ambitious and capable in some aspects of my work because I know I can get a head start using AI. But note: I am the one who came up with the idea, and I needed to describe the problem and some of the necessary steps. And, importantly, I am the one responsible if something breaks along the way, and so I need to have a strategy to confirm that everything made it into the finished project successfully.
I think the following is very much in the spirit of coding in 2026: Think of LLMs as your extremely fast, extremely well-read, overconfident junior collaborator. You can use them to quickly retrieve information, you can ask them to help you write code, they can help troubleshoot problems. But ultimately, you are setting the expectations (specifications), and you are responsible for the project (so you better do some verification). And, further, there will be times when you have to show that you, too, actually know how to do the stuff (the checkpoints).


One more term you’ll see a lot: an agent is capable of actually making changes on your computer — creating new folders, creating/editing files, maybe sending emails — rather than giving you text in a web browser that you have to move around. Still basically a junior collaborator: you still provide the details and check the results, you just have to do less manual labor.

Answer these:

Two students give an LLM the identical prompt for a projectile program. Predict: (a) identical code, (b) different code, same numerical answers, (c) different code, possibly different answers. Write one sentence defending your pick.
The LLM hands you a projectile program and it runs without any errors, and produces a nice plot. List every distinct reason you can think of that its output might still be wrong.

title: Getting going in your language
text: This page contains my recommendations for how to set up your programming environment. You can do this entire course in Google Colab and MATLAB Online — nothing to install, works on any machine. But at some point you might decide running Python/MATLAB on your own machine is a good idea. Programs run faster, you can see all the files in a project easier, and it just feels better to have everything in a real editor.

title: Getting going in your language
text:
Python via Google Colab
Go to colab.research.google.com, sign in with your university Google account, click New notebook, and… that’s it. Python runs on Google’s computers; NumPy, matplotlib, and pandas are pre-installed. Notebooks are saved on your Google Drive. It is a little bit clumsy to handle files (e.g. a csv) but we will figure it out!


We’ll talk about how to import packages soon… engineers don’t use base Python much, we need to bring in some extra tools.

title: Getting going in your language
text:
Python on your machine
There are multiple avenues here, and if you are confident enough to find your own way (e.g., with pip), I believe in you. In general, there are two things you’ll need to do: install Python+a package manager, and install an editor.

Package manager
My recommendation is to install miniconda — NOT the full Anaconda (which you can find nearby if you really want to, but I’m not linking it).


The full Anaconda is attractive: it has everything you will need in one install, but also a lot of unnecessary stuff. I grew to hate the navigator and the way it insisted on cross-checking all the packages every time I updated, and so I “downgraded” to miniconda (which still cross-checks, but there are way fewer packages). Additionally, I am not fond of the IDEs (Integrated Development Environment) that come with Anaconda. I much prefer VS Code, which supports Jupyter Notebooks and has a GitHub integration.
Miniconda installs Python, but otherwise I think there are zero packages, so you’ll install what you need from the command line. NumPy, matplotlib, and pandas are necessary for this course; this page has the instructions. Note that miniconda still uses conda as the command.


What are “packages”? They are collections Python files that include useful Python functions that can be “called”. For example: someone has already written an implementation of the Trapezoid Rule for finding the area under a curve, and implemented it into the SciPy package. Now, instead of writing the code from scratch, you can just call that function with trapezoid(y) in your code.

pip is another package-management option — not that different from conda. If you have reason to go that way, do it; plenty of tutorials around.







Tip



Some other packages that might be worth installing:

Jupyter is a “notebook” environment that looks a lot like Colab.
Seaborn is built on-top of matplotlib… it makes really beautiful plots.
SciPy is a toolbox of numerical routines — differential equation solvers, integrators, etc. It is a very large package but has a lot of very good tools that are used in engineering.
Scikit-learn is a good machine learning toolbox, we might use it in a Machine Learning Side Quest.





Editor
For the editor, I recommend VS Code — it supports Jupyter notebooks (and it’s notebook interface is better than the default Jupyter interface), has an integrated terminal, and has GitHub integration. Install VS Code, then its Python and Jupyter extensions (VS Code will automatically offer to install them the first time you open a .py or .ipynb file).


GitHub is a website that hosts code projects (“repositories”) so you can save your work, track changes over time, and share it with others.
If you would like to install a different editor, and feel confident in doing so, go ahead! One example: Google Antigravity is apparently quite similar to VS Code. (I haven’t tried it yet!)






NotePython “environments” (optional reading)





Many serious programmers insist each project should have its own “environment” with a unique set of packages. For example, TensorFlow apparently does not play nice with NumPy version 2.0 or higher, and so folks who use TensorFlow will likely have an isolated environment for it where NumPy 1.9x is installed. (Even after reverting to NumPy 1.9x, I still couldn’t get TensorFlow to work, but that is beside the point!) For this class, it should not be a big deal to work entirely in the base environment.
If you do want to create separate environments, e.g., one for each project, you can. From the command line, you would start with something like conda create --name project1 and then conda activate project1 puts you in that environment, and then conda install numpy would get you numpy in just that environment. You need to install packages in each environment – if you have three environments set up on your machine, you might technically have NumPy installed three times.

Welcome to MCEN 1030: Introduction to Engineering Computing, taught by Professor Jeremy Koch in the Fall 2026 semester.
When I took this course (in Fall 2006… oof), the big challenge for students was to figure out how to use fundamental programming ideas — loops, conditional statements, indexing — to achieve an engineering task. My professor gave very clean problem statements so that we could focus on writing the code, and we spent hours figuring out how to put the ideas in the right order, getting the syntax right, and debugging errors.
Today, we have AI (artificial intelligence), specifically LLMs (large language models). These have proven to be extremely capable of writing code based on a prompt (natural language instructions). Engineers need some understanding of how computation can be used in their projects, but they are not manually typing in for i in items: anymore… they are writing prompts that include something like “iterate through the items in that list” and having an LLM do the work.
What does that mean for an introduction to engineering computing class, if traditional problems have been conquered by AI? We still need to learn what is possible with computation…
how computer logic works…
and how to interpret code…
but we will also learn how to integrate LLMs into our workflow. Importantly, we are not going to treat LLM-generated code as a “black box”1: we need to understand what is going on in our code. After all, if you end up using an LLM-generated result in your job and something explodes, you won’t be able to blame an LLM — it’s your fault!
Further, we’ll learn why LLMs are not 100% trustworthy and will see that they, too, often produce broken code. That doesn’t mean we give up on the project — if we understand how to talk about computational ideas, how to interpret results, and how to troubleshoot/debug, we can work with an LLM. The net effect will likely be that we produce better work, faster, as long as we humans are an active participant in the process.

title: Welcome
text:
The big idea
The process of creating computational tools looks roughly like this:

  The computational pipeline
  Five boxes in a row: Idea, Specification, Production, Verification, Use, connected by arrows. A curved arrow labeled Adaptation loops from Use back to Specification.
  
    
      
    
  
  
    
    Idea
    
    Specification
    
    Production
    
    Verification
    
    Use
    
    
    
    
    
    Adaptation
  

For decades, Production — thinking about the code elements, structure, and syntax, and doing the typing — was the bottleneck, and so intro courses like this one spent nearly all their time on it. That bottleneck is gone: AI tools produce working code (from a good description) in seconds. The new bottlenecks are the two highlighted boxes:
Specification means describing the problem precisely: the inputs and outputs, what has to happen in the middle, what to do at the edges. If you can’t articulate the problem, no tool — human or AI — can solve it for you.
Verification means refusing to trust a black box: sanity-checking results against hand estimates, testing edge cases, knowing the ways a program (or a model, or an AI) goes wrong.
You will still read and run and modify plenty of code in this course — you can’t verify what you can’t read. But you will be graded on whether you can think computationally: frame a problem, direct the tools, and audit the results. That is what engineers actually do!

title: HW 4 · The siren
text:
The model
A siren that’s coming toward you sounds higher than it really is, and one that’s moving away sounds lower. If a siren moves at speed \(U\) along a straight road, emits a true frequency \(f_0\), and passes closest to the microphone at time \(t_\text{pass}\), at a distance \(y_0\), then the microphone hears an “observed frequency”
\[
f_\text{obs}(t) = \frac{f_0}{1 - \dfrac{U}{c}\cos\theta(t)}, \qquad \cos(\theta(t)) = \frac{-U\,(t - t_\text{pass})}{\sqrt{U^2 (t-t_\text{pass})^2 + y_0^2}}
\]
where \(c = 343\) m/s is the speed of sound. Let’s confirm this equation matches our intuition:

Long before the pass, \(t - t_\text{pass}\) is a large negative number, so \(\cos\theta \approx +1\), the denominator is a bit less than 1, and \(f_\text{obs}\) is a bit more than \(f_0\). Approaching, higher pitch. ✓
Long after the pass, \(\cos\theta \approx -1\) and the pitch is lower. ✓
Right at \(t_\text{pass}\), \(\cos\theta = 0\) and we hear exactly \(f_0\).

Count the unknowns: \(U\), \(f_0\), \(y_0\), \(t_\text{pass}\)… four things we don’t know, but we’ll figure them out from the data.

title: HW 4 · The siren
text:
Part 1 — Look first
Load the file and plot it: markers, not lines, since these are measurements; labels with units. Before any fitting, just look at it and write down what you see.
Two of the four unknowns can be read nearly straight off this plot. Which two, and roughly what are their values? (Hint: what can we learn from the middle?) Reading them by eye is fine. Write both readings in a text cell, with units. You’ll use them in Part 4.

title: HW 4 · The siren
section: Part 2 — The model as a function
text:
Part 2 — The model as a function
Write siren_freq(t, U, f0, y0, t_pass), which returns the predicted frequency at each time in the array t. Write a docstring with units.
Check it in isolation before you trust it. Use these made-up values, not the siren data: \(U = 20\) m/s, \(f_0 = 500\) Hz, \(y_0 = 10\) m, \(t_\text{pass} = 3\) s. Then do three checks, each in its own code cell:

Call the function at t = 3 and confirm it returns 500.
Call it at t = -1000 and t = 1000, stand-ins for “long before” and “long after.” Work out \(f_0 / (1 - U/c)\) and \(f_0 / (1 + U/c)\) with a calculator, show the arithmetic in a text cell, and compare.
Plot it for t = np.linspace(0, 6, 200) and confirm the curve goes down as time goes on, not up.

title: HW 4 · The siren
section: Part 3 — An estimate with no fitting at all
text:
Part 3 — An estimate with no fitting at all
Before we build anything clever, let’s get a number we can check against.
Far from the pass, the curve levels off into two flat stretches: a high one on the way in and a low one on the way out. Write code to do some averaging: take the mean of the first 20 frequencies and call it \(f_+\). Take the mean of the last 20 and call it \(f_-\). That’s one line each, using slicing ([:20] and [-20:]) and .mean() from week 4. Print both.
Now go back to the two limits in the model, \(f_+ = f_0/(1 - U/c)\) and \(f_- = f_0/(1 + U/c)\). That’s two equations with two unknowns (\(U\) and \(f_0\)). Solve them for \(U\) and \(f_0\) using algebra, not code. Write the steps in a text cell, then plug in your \(f_+\) and \(f_-\) with one line of Python each. Write down both estimates.

title: HW 4 · The siren
section: Part 4 — The sweep as a search
text:
Part 4 — The sweep as a search
We will write a basic “fitting” process to determine the “best fit to the data”. The idea is to guess \(U\), \(f_0\), \(y_0\), and \(t_\text{pass}\), and then see how well the resulting equation replicates the data. Then guess another set of values and check, then guess another set and check… . It won’t be random guessing though — we will be systematic, sweeping through a reasonable range for the values. The tricky thing is: we need a way to score the guesses so that we can identify the best one.
Let’s do the following:

Decide on a way to keep score. For one set of guesses, run siren_freq at every time in the file and compare it with the measured frequencies. Boil the mismatch down to one number, where smaller means better. How you calculate that number is up to you (it’s a spec decision).






Caution



Simply adding up the differences doesn’t work — positive and negative differences cancel each other out.


Make the problem smaller. If we did a sweep over all four unknowns, with 40 possible values each, it would be 2.5 million guesses. That is not that crazy, but let’s simplify: we’ll hold \(t_\text{pass}\) and \(f_0\) fixed. Use your Part 1 estimate for \(t_\text{pass}\). For \(f_0\), use either your Part 1 estimate or the value your Part 3 algebra gives, and say which in your spec. Now you only have to sweep \(U\) and \(y_0\).
Create a “nested loop”. We can put a for loop inside a for loop:






Let’s do that: loop over \(U\), and loop over \(y_0\) inside that loop. Every \((U,y_0)\) pair needs a score. As you go, keep track of the best score so far and the \(U\) and \(y_0\) that produced it.

Choosing the search ranges is part of your spec. Part 3 tells you roughly where \(U\) is, so search around it. For \(y_0\), the plot won’t tell you directly. The microphone was “set back some distance” from the road, which could mean 1 m or 100 m. You can always start with something coarse and run a finer sweep around the best spot afterward.
Write the sweep results to a file, siren_sweep.csv: three columns (\(U\), \(y_0\), score) with units in the header, and one row per guess. A 40 × 40 sweep, for example, is a 1,600-row file (plus header).






Tip



The nested loop makes this slightly awkward, because i alone no longer tells you which row you’re on. One way: pre-allocate three arrays of length (number of \(U\) values) × (number of \(y_0\) values). Then initialize a counter k = 0 before the loops, fill slot k of each array, and do k = k + 1 as the very last step in the inner loop.


Then np.savetxt the three arrays side by side. Peek at the first few lines only, e.g. print(open("siren_sweep.csv").read()[:200]). Printing thousands of rows will turn into dozens of pages of numbers in your PDF.

title: HW 4 · The siren
text:
Part 5 — How sure are you?
Plot the data and your best-fit curve together: data as markers, model as a line. Then answer these three questions:

How good is the best fit? Compare two numbers, both in Hz:

The noise. Run .std() on the first 20 frequencies. (The standard deviation: roughly, how far a typical point sits from the average of its neighbors. New function, same idea as .mean().)
The fit’s typical miss. At your best \(U\) and \(y_0\), compute the differences between model and data, square them, take the mean, then the square root. (If that’s what your score already was, you’re done. If you picked a different score, compute this one anyway so the two numbers are comparable.)

Are they about the same size, or is the miss clearly bigger? If it’s clearly bigger, something in your model is a little off. Which of the two values you held fixed is the likeliest culprit, and why? (Answering that is required. Actually re-sweeping to fix it is optional.)
Which parameter is the fit least sure about? Make two plots. First, hold \(U\) at its best value and plot the score against \(y_0\). Second, hold \(y_0\) at its best value and plot the score against \(U\). You can pull these from your sweep file, or recompute along each line with a finer step (which gives a smoother plot). On each, find how far you can move away from the best value before the score gets 10% worse than the best score. Write that as a percentage of the best value, e.g. “±4%.” The parameter with the bigger percentage is the one that is less certain.
Based on our data and the fit to the observed frequency equation, what do we know about how the ambulance was moving? What things do we not know — i.e., what aspects of the motion are not captured in the data?

title: HW 2 · Which way should the panel point?
text:
The model
Technically the panel orientation requires two angular measurements. Think about starting with it pointing upwards, and then tilting it until it faces due south (we adjusted one angular coordinate), and then rotating it around so that it faces east (we adjusted the second angular coordinate). We’ll simplify a bit and focus on just solar noon, eliminating the second angle from our worries.
A tilted panel collects energy in proportion to how squarely it faces the sun. If the sunlight arrives at an angle \(\theta\) away from straight-on, the panel collects a factor of \(\cos\theta\) less than it would if the sun were directly overhead of it. Let \(\alpha\) be the sun’s elevation above the horizon and \(\beta\) the panel’s tilt up from horizontal. The sun’s angle from straight-up (the zenith angle) is \(90° - \alpha\), and the panel’s normal is tilted \(\beta\) from straight-up, so
\[
\theta = \left|\,(90° - \alpha) - \beta\,\right|
\]
and the power the panel produces is
\[
P = G \cdot A \cdot \eta \cdot \cos\theta
\]
with \(G\) the incoming sunlight in W/m², \(A = 1.6\) m² the panel area, and \(\eta = 0.20\) the conversion efficiency.


This model ignores diffuse light from the sky, reflections off the roof, the fact that panels get less efficient when hot, and everything that happens away from solar noon.






Tip



Two notes on using this in code. NumPy’s np.cos expects radians, not degrees, but np.radians(theta) will do the conversion for you. And np.abs gives you the absolute value elementwise on a whole array.

title: HW 2 · Which way should the panel point?
section: Part 1 — Build the function and check it by hand
text:
Part 1 — Build the function and check it by hand
Write panel_power(tilt_deg, elevation_deg) returning watts, with G, A, and \(\eta\) as arguments with sensible defaults. Write a docstring: what goes in, in what units, what comes out.
Then verify it in isolation before you use it for anything (this is standard P1). On the equinox at Boulder, the sun’s noon elevation is \(\alpha = 50°\). Compute \(P\) by hand for a tilt of \(0°\) and for a tilt of \(40°\) — write down the arithmetic, not just the answers — and confirm the function agrees. If it doesn’t, the function is wrong!






Tip



One of those two hand cases is arithmetically trivial. That’s a good strategy: pick inputs whose answer you can get without a calculator. You’ll be more inclined to verify the easy cases, and less inclined to make mistakes!

title: HW 2 · Which way should the panel point?
text:
Part 2 — Sweep the tilt
Build a NumPy array of tilt angles from \(0°\) to \(90°\), evaluate panel_power on the whole array in one line, and find the best tilt using argmax. Plot power against tilt, with axis labels and units. There is basically no cost to doing a lot of points here: you could calculate at every degree… 91 points is not that many.
Then the sanity check:






Important



There’s a rule of thumb that a fixed panel should be tilted at roughly the site’s latitude. Boulder is at 40°N. Does your sweep agree?
If it does — say so explicitly, and explain in a sentence or two why the model produces that result, using the geometry above. “It matched” is not the finding; being able to say why it had to match is. (Hint: look at the equation.)
If it doesn’t, you have a bug, and the two usual suspects are degrees-versus-radians and a sign error in \(\theta\). Find it.


Two follow-ups, one calculation each:

Winter solstice drops the noon sun to \(\alpha = 26.5°\); summer solstice raises it to \(73.5°\). Rerun the sweep for each. Do the best tilts make physical sense to you? Which of the three best tilts would you pick, if you had to pick one?
Extend your tilt array past \(90°\), out to \(180°\) — a panel tipped over past vertical until it’s face-down. What does the function report, and is it physically possible? Say what the function should do there and why it doesn’t.
