title: Practice Library
text:
Tracing (week 2)
T1. Look through the code and try to predict all three printed values, then run to check.







Make a two-column table of a and b values, then go line-by-line. Remember: = means is assigned — line 3 uses the values as they are at that moment.


10, 4, 6.

After line 1: a is 6.
After line 2: b is 4 (and a is still 6).
After Line 3: a is 6+4, that is: a is 10. (And b stays 4 — it stored a value, not a relationship.)


T2. This one prints a single value.







The same line twice is not the same result twice — the second one starts from where the first one left off.


16. First squaring: 4. Second squaring squares the new value: 16.

title: Practice Library
text:
Logic: if/elif/else (week 2)
L1.







Go top to bottom, and the first true branch wins. Check the boundaries: is 100 greater than 100?


highway, highway (100 is not > 100), too fast, city (−5 falls through to else… not sure this was a good specification, if we are talking about the speed of a city!).

L2. Here’s a function that sanity-checks a thermometer reading before we trust it. Predict all four outputs.







or is True if either side is True. And watch the last one closely: is −40 less than −40?


ok, impossible, suspicious, ok.
The −999 is worth a second look. It’s a common “missing data” marker in real files (we saw one in the wind speeds in week 4), and it’s below absolute zero, so it gets caught by the first branch. If the branches were in the other order it would only get called “suspicious,” which undersells it a bit.

L3. Pipe flow is laminar below a Reynolds number of about 2300, turbulent above about 4000, and transitional in between. (Those are just three labels for three ranges of a number. No fluid mechanics needed today.) Predict what flow_regime(10000) returns, then fix the function.







10000 is greater than 2300. Once a branch is True, does Python ever look at the ones below it?


It returns "transitional". The turbulent branch can never run: anything above 4000 is also above 2300, and the first branch grabs it. Two fixes, either is fine:
# check the biggest threshold first
if Re > 4000:
    return "turbulent"
elif Re > 2300:
    return "transitional"
else:
    return "laminar"
or keep the original order but make the middle branch say exactly what it means: if Re > 2300 and Re <= 4000:. The first is more common. With elif chains, the order is part of the logic.

title: Practice Library
text:
Functions (week 3)
F1. Fill in the blank ______ so the function matches its docstring, then verify it works by running the code.







Area is π r² — and remember Python needs the power written explicitly.


return 3.14159 * r ** 2      # or: 3.14159 * r * r

F2. Predict what prints.







The n inside the function is limited in scope. What happens in the function stays in the function — only the return value escapes.


1 then 11. The outer n is untouched; add_ten worked on its own local copy and returned the result.

title: Practice Library
text:
Arrays (week 4)
A1. Fill in the blank so t holds the fall time for every height at once, then print it.







The formula is \(t=\sqrt{2h/g}\), and NumPy’s square root is np.sqrt(...). Write the arithmetic as if h were a single number — the array handles the “for every value” part itself.


t = np.sqrt(2 * h / 9.81)
The first entry should be ≈ 0.45 s and each height is 4× the previous, so each time should be 2× the previous (√4 = 2).

title: Practice Library
text:
Loops (weeks 4–5)

Looping over values, looping over indices
X1. Fix the loop so it prints the sum of the squares of 1 through 4. (What value do you expect?)







Run it as-is and look at what you get: 16. The loop isn’t accumulating — each pass throws away the previous total. What’s missing from the right-hand side?


total = total + k * k
The accumulator pattern: the new total is built from the old total. total = k * k just overwrites, and you end up with only the last pass (16).

X2. Assembly problem: these lines compute the average of a list, but they’re scrambled. Reorder them (cut and paste in the editor) so it runs and prints 5.0.








Names must exist before they’re used.
The indented line belongs to the for.
The print needs everything finished.

(Also — could you avoid hard-coding count = 3? Python’s len(values) exists and is probably better.)


values = [3, 5, 7]
total = 0
count = 3
for v in values:
    total = total + v
print(total / count)
The first three lines can go in any order among themselves.

X3. Two loops over the same list. Predict everything that prints — both loops.







What is len(tilts)? Then what’s range of that? The first loop hands you the things in the list; the second hands you positions, and you have to go look up the thing yourself.


20
30
40
0 20
1 30
2 40
range(len(tilts)) is range(3), which is 0, 1, 2: every valid index. Same three values come out either way. So why would anyone bother with the index version? See the next one.

X4. We have two parallel lists: the voltage and current of four devices. Fill in the blank so the loop prints each device’s power, \(P = VI\).







A for v in volts: loop would hand you each voltage… but then how would you find the matching current? The index i is the thing that ties volts[i] to amps[i]. How many indices do you need?


for i in range(len(volts)):
Prints 24.0 W, 6.0 W, 5.0 W, 0.66 W. This is the reason to loop over indices: you need the same position in two (or more) lists at once.
(Just giving you some vocabulary if you want to read more: Python also has zip, as in for v, a in zip(volts, amps):, which walks two lists side by side. An LLM will hand you that one a lot. Same idea, different spelling.)



Collecting results with append
X5. Fill in the two blanks so times ends up holding the fall time for each height.







The first blank needs to make an empty list, before the loop. The second blank sticks t on the end of that list, once per pass.


times = []
...
    times.append(t)
Three heights in, three times out: len(times) is 3. Sanity check: a 1 m drop taking about 0.45 s feels right (drop your keys… that’s roughly how long it takes). And 20 m is 4× higher than 5 m, so it should take 2× as long, which it does.

X6. Someone moved one line. Predict what prints.







That results = [] line runs every pass now. What does it do to whatever was already in results?


[40.0]. Every pass makes a brand-new empty list and puts one thing in it, so at the end only the last pass survives. The empty list has to be built before the loop, so it can survive all the passes.



Loops with if inside
X7. A wind sensor logs -999.0 whenever it misses a reading. Fill in the condition so only the real readings get collected.







Several conditions work: “not equal to −999,” or “at least zero” (can a wind speed be negative?). sum and len are built into Python and work on plain lists.


if v != -999.0:      # or: if v >= 0:
good is [8.1, 10.7, 9.8, 7.4] and the average is 9.0 m/s.
Now try it with the if removed, so every value gets appended. The average comes out to −327 m/s: a wind blowing backwards at roughly the speed of sound. Nobody needs to read the code to know that’s wrong — which is the whole point of estimating before you trust a number.

X8. Counting is just an accumulator that adds 1. How many of these daily highs (°C) are above 32? Fill in the blank.







Same shape as total = total + x, but what are we adding each time we find a hot day?


hot_days = hot_days + 1
Prints 3 (33, 35, 34). Swap the 7 numbers for a century of Boulder summers and this is, more-or-less, one way to ask “are hot days getting more common?”

X9. The “best so far” pattern. Predict what prints. Then change output[3] to 320 (a tie!) and predict again. Then change > to >= and predict a third time.







Keep a table with one column: best_i. It only changes when the current output beats the best one so far. Does “ties” count as beating?


Original: 40 320.
With the tie and >: still 40 320. When i is 3, 320 > 320 is False, so the first 320 keeps its spot.
With the tie and >=: 50 320. Now a tie does count, so the later one takes over.
This is exactly what output.argmax() does for you in one line (and NumPy picks the first one on a tie, like >). Writing it by hand is worth doing once, because the loop version can do things argmax can’t, like “the best one we can afford.” See the last problem on this page.

X10. Here are positions logged during a phone drop (onto a pillow, please), every 0.1 s. The loop estimates the velocity between each pair of neighboring readings. Predict the printed values — roughly is fine — and figure out why the range starts at 1.







range(1, 5) is 1, 2, 3, 4 — it starts at 1 instead of 0. Each pass uses the reading at i and the one just before it, at i-1. What would i-1 be on a pass where i is 0?


0.1 -0.49
0.2 -1.47
0.3 -2.45
0.4 -3.44
A physics check: the velocity should get about \(g\,\Delta t = 9.81 \times 0.1 \approx 0.98\) m/s more negative every step, and it does (−0.49, −1.47, −2.45, …). Negative, because we measure \(y\) upward and the phone is going down. Good.
Why start at 1? If i were 0, then y[i-1] is y[-1], the last reading. Python happily does that (negative indices are legal!) and you’d get a “velocity” of about −1.96 m/s at t = 0, when the phone hadn’t started moving yet. No error, just a wrong number. (Also notice that five positions give only four velocities. Off-by-one, our old friend.)

title: Practice Library
text:
Simulation (week 5)
S1. A cup of coffee cools faster when it’s much hotter than the room, and slower as it gets close. A time-stepped version: each minute, the temperature drops by a fraction k of the gap between the coffee and the room. Trace it and predict the three printed lines.







First pass: the gap is 90 − 20 = 70, and 10% of that is 7. The second pass starts from wherever the first one left off.


0 83.0
1 76.7
2 71.03
The drops are 7, then 6.3, then 5.67: shrinking, because the gap shrinks. That’s the “slows down as it gets close” behavior we wanted.

S2. Now let’s break it on purpose. Same cooling model, but someone got impatient and took fifteen-minute steps. Run it. What’s wrong with the answer, physically?







Look at the first printed temperature. Can coffee sitting in a 20 °C room get colder than the room?


0 -15.0
1 37.5
2 11.25
Frozen coffee, in a warm room, which then bounces back up to 37.5 and down again. A real cup never goes below room temperature. The algebra is fine. The problem is that k * dt is now 1.5, so each step “removes” 150% of the gap and overshoots. Small steps keep the model honest. (Try dt = 5.0: it’s off from the dt = 1 answer, but at least it’s not absurd.)

S3. After a falling-ball simulation, we want the time when the ball first goes below the ground. Fill in the blank, using a mask from week 4 (no new loop needed).







Build it in pieces. y < 0 is an array of True/False. t[y < 0] is every time when the ball was underground. You want the first one of those.


t_hit = t[y < 0][0]
Prints 1.44. The exact answer from \(t = \sqrt{2h/g}\) is 1.43 s. Close, and our stepped answer is a hair late, which makes sense: the simulation always uses the speed from the start of each step, so it’s always a little slower than the real ball.

title: Practice Library
text:
Files and tables (week 6)
D1. Four days of weather, one row per day: day number, high (°C), low (°C). Predict all five printed things.







data[row, column], both counting from zero. A : means “all of them.” And swing is the high minus the low for every day at once.



(4, 3): four rows, three columns.
18.2: row 2 is the third day, column 1 is the high.
[1. 2. 3. 4.]: the whole first column, the day numbers.
12.4: last row, low column.
2.0: the swings are 15.3, 15.7, 12.2, 10.1, so the biggest is at index 1, and row 1’s day number is 2. (Boulder in the fall really does swing 15 °C in a day. Not a typo.)

title: Practice Library
text:
pandas (week 7)
P1. Some made-up summer highs for two years (made up, so don’t draw climate conclusions from them!). Fill in the two blanks: the average high for each year, and the number of months with a high above 29 °C.







“For each year” is the phrase that means groupby. For the second one: filter first, df[df["high_C"] > 29], then count the rows of what’s left with len(...).


print(df.groupby("year")["high_C"].mean())
print(len(df[df["high_C"] > 29]))
1950 averages 28.1 °C and 2020 averages about 29.67 °C. Three months are above 29 (29.8, 31.2, 29.9).
Does this mean it’s warming? Two years of three months each, invented by me, is not a trend. It’s an anecdote with a decimal point. The real question needs the real century of data, and a plot.

title: Practice Library
text:
Dictionaries (week 8)
DI1. A solar panel, described as a dictionary. Predict every line of output.







Assigning to a key that already exists replaces its value. Assigning to a key that doesn’t exist yet… try it and see. (len of a dictionary counts its keys.)



400
210.5263157894737, watts per square meter of panel. Sanity check: full sunlight delivers roughly 1000 W/m², so this panel turns about 21% of it into electricity. That’s a realistic number for a modern panel, so the dictionary is probably not lying to us.
35, because the old 40 got replaced.
5: assigning to a new key adds it. This is how you build up a dictionary one piece at a time.
The whole dictionary, now with 'cost_usd': 220 on the end.


DI2. Here’s a (shortened) reply from an hourly weather forecast API. It’s a dictionary, with dictionaries inside, with lists inside those. Fill in the blanks.







Read the path like directions: go to "hourly", then inside that go to "temperature_2m". The units live somewhere else — in "hourly_units".


temps = forecast["hourly"]["temperature_2m"]
...
print(forecast["hourly_units"]["temperature_2m"])
Prints 19.6, °C, and 2026-10-13T14:00.
Notice "time" and "temperature_2m" are two parallel lists, just like diameters and totals in week 4: index 2 in one goes with index 2 in the other. That’s why the last line works.

DI3. Looping over a dictionary hands you its keys, one at a time. Predict the output (roughly), then add titanium (4500 kg/m³) to the dictionary and run it again.







On the first pass material is "steel", so density[material] is density["steel"]. Then 7850 × 0.002 is…


Steel 15.7 kg, aluminum 5.4 kg, wood 1.2 kg. To add titanium, put "titanium": 4500 in the curly braces (or write density["titanium"] = 4500 before the loop, like in DI1). It comes out at 9.0 kg.
Sanity check: 2 liters of water is 2 kg. Wood is lighter than that (it floats!), and steel is about 8× heavier, which is about right if you’ve ever picked up a dumbbell.
You probably saw steel print as 15.700000000000001. That’s not a bug in our code. Computers store decimals in binary, and some decimals (like 0.002) can’t be stored exactly, so a tiny bit of fuzz shows up way out at the end. It’s harmless here. Use round(mass, 2) if it bugs you.

DI4. A logger collected four replies from the ISS API. One request failed, and one came back with a key missing. Predict everything that prints, including the final list.







Go one reply at a time. Does this reply have a "latitude" key? If not, the append line fails, and Python jumps to except without running the print("ok").


ok
skipped: KeyError('latitude')
ok
skipped: KeyError('latitude')
[51.45, 50.98]
Four replies in, two latitudes out, and the loop survived both failures. Something to chew on: suppose we were also collecting timestamp in its own list. The last reply has a timestamp. If we appended it before trying the latitude, the two lists would end up different lengths… and they’d no longer be parallel.

title: Practice Library
text:
Putting it together
Z1. We’re choosing a wind turbine rotor diameter. Bigger rotors make more power, but they also cost more, and we have a budget of $3.5 million. Fill in the condition so the loop finds the most powerful turbine we can afford.







Two things have to be true at once for a turbine to become the new best: it’s affordable, and it beats the best one so far. “At once” is the word and.


if costs[i] <= budget and P > best_P:
Prints 100 m rotor: 1767 kW. The 110 and 120 m rotors make more power but cost too much.
This is the thing argmax alone can’t do: it would cheerfully pick the 120 m rotor, which we can’t buy. Here a function, a loop over indices, parallel lists, if, and, and the best-so-far pattern all show up in about ten lines, and that’s basically a real (if tiny) design decision.
A quick check that the numbers are plausible: real 100 m wind turbines are typically rated around 2–3 MW (at higher wind speeds than our 10 m/s), so 1.8 MW is in the right neighborhood.

title: What do engineers do with computation?
text: We’re starting with computational thinking, not coding. What is actually possible with computation? What does a computer need from you to do something useful? How can you tell if a calculation is trustworthy? These are things we’ll be thinking about all semester, but we’ll introduce them here.

title: What do engineers do with computation?
text:
Think First
Recall

Think of a time you gave someone instructions (directions to your house, a recipe, rules to a game) and they got it wrong. Whose fault was it?
In high school physics, you checked answers by asking “is this number reasonable?” — a car going 900 m/s is probably a mistake. What was that process like… what were you recalling, what did you do when you realized the answer was ridiculous?

Look Ahead

If an AI can write working code from a plain-English description in five seconds, what’s left for the engineer to do?
What would it take for you to trust a program you didn’t write?
crumbs: What do engineers do with computation?

title: What do engineers do with computation?
section: Four things you may not know are possible with computation
text:
Four things you may not know are possible with computation
Predict every outcome of a process. Write a function that models something — the stress in a bracket, the temperature of a battery — then use that function 100 times with 100 different inputs and write every result to a file. Runtime: about one second. You have just explored the entire design space of a product before building anything.


A function has a very similar meaning in this class as it did in algebra: there are inputs, and there are outputs. An example: we might want to calculate the area of a triangle. We’d write a function with inputs base and height, and the output is the area. In Python, this would look like
def triangle_area(base, height):
    return 0.5 * base * height
If we “called” this function and provided values for base and height, it would “return” the area of the triangle. We’ll talk about this structure a lot more in two weeks.
Handle data at engineering scale. A test rig logging 100 readings per second produces 360,000 rows an hour. Excel is not going to help you here. The tools in this course handle that with ease.
Collect and process real engineering data. From a few lines of code you can pull the live position of the International Space Station, read the accelerometer inside your own phone, or send a question to an AI and use its answer inside your program.
Solve the unsolvable. Most real equations in engineering have no analytical solution. Many of those problems can be solved numerically in 10 lines of code.
crumbs: What do engineers do with computation?

title: What do engineers do with computation?
text:
The pipeline
Creating a computational tool looks something like this:

  The computational pipeline
  Five boxes in a row: Idea, Specification, Production, Verification, Use, connected by arrows. A curved arrow labeled Adaptation loops from Use back to Specification.
  
    
      
    
  
  
    
    Idea
    
    Specification
    
    Production
    
    Verification
    
    Use
    
    
    
    
    
    Adaptation
  

The idea is always the hard part. Then, at least for the seventy years after that, production was the bottleneck: writing correct code takes time, and intro courses like this one were traditionally spent almost entirely on how to write correct code.
That era is over. AI tools now produce working code from a good description in seconds. Production has, for most everyday engineering purposes, been solved.


John Backus thought of himself as a bad assembly-language coder, so in the 1950s he created FORTRAN. The history of computer science is a story of making code less abstract, and LLMs might be the next step.
What should be the focus today?

title: What do engineers do with computation?
section: Specification means describing the problem completely
text:
Specification means describing the problem completely
… the inputs, the outputs, what should happen in between, and what should happen at the edges. It sounds trivial, but it is where real engineering projects most often fail: whether it’s an AI, a contractor, or a teammate who is helping with the task, every gap in your specification gets filled with an assumption. If your specification doesn’t mention a material, maybe the ideal gas assumption is made — problematic when you are talking about oil flowing through a pipeline!
Think about asking a question like…

“Tell me the average temperature in Boulder.”







NoteWhat details do you actually need to provide?





Average over what — the whole century of records, one year, one month? Average of the daily highs, the daily lows, or the midpoint between them (which is what “average temperature” usually means, but maybe you are concerned with human comfort and thus should pay attention to the extremes)? What about the days the weather station didn’t report anything? There are plenty of those if we’re looking back to the 1890s. In the raw file, a missing day might not be blank, it might be recorded as -9999. Hand that to a basic Python program for computing the average and you might “learn” that the average temperature is about −270 °C. And, a classic problem even for humans: What are the units?



Now a different kind of gap. Compare these two problem statements:

A. “Write a function freq_shift(t, U, x0, y0, c, f) that returns the apparent frequency of a moving siren at each time in the array t, and plots it against time.”


B. “Write a program that would allow you to determine the velocity (speed and direction) of a siren.”

Statement A is a completed specification — someone already did all the thinking, and you’re just following instructions. Statement B is a problem. To attack B, you have to decide: what are the inputs my team has access to/ability to control? (A recording? Frequency-vs-time data? Hypothetical object speeds?) What physics connects frequency to velocity? What are the unknowns? What should the program output, and in what form? What if the data is noisy?
In the old version of this course, where we focused on code production, I’d give you Statement A. (Indeed, this was a homework problem last year.) In this version, where we augment our work with LLMs, you might get Statement B. Importantly: in real engineering, no one will hand you Statement A, especially now that LLMs make short work of the ensuing code. Producing Statement A from Statement B is the job.

title: What do engineers do with computation?
section: Verification means confirming a program does what you intended
text:
Verification means confirming a program does what you intended
… and notably: not assuming that the product given to you by a colleague or LLM is correct. This semester we will verify our code with:
The hand estimate: before running anything, compute a rough expected answer for a simple case. A dropped wrench falls 3 meters in about \(t = \sqrt{2h/g} \approx \sqrt{2(3~\text{m})/(9.8~\text{m/s}^2)} \approx 0.8\) seconds. If the program says 12 seconds, the program is wrong. If it says 0.78 seconds, that’s a good sign.
The edge case: what happens at zero? At a negative input? When the file is empty? What should happen in these cases?
The intuition check: you have years of physical intuition — heavier things don’t fall faster, sirens sound higher approaching than receding, hot coffee cools to room temperature over several minutes but won’t drop below room temperature. That intuition is a verification instrument. Perhaps unexpectedly: we will be practicing our physical intuition in this programming course!






Important



An AI will hand you code that runs yet is confidently, invisibly wrong — it flipped a sign, used the wrong equation because you forgot to specify one, assumed Celsius when the data was in Fahrenheit. It will not warn you. “It ran without errors” and “it is correct” are entirely different claims.

title: What do engineers do with computation?
text:
The map of this course
Four verbs describe what engineers do with computation, and they outline this course:

Fetch — get real data into (and out of) your programs: sensors, files, the internet.
Process — turn raw data into meaningful quantities: functions, sweeps, big datasets.
Simulate — build models, make predictions, ask “what if,” and know when not to believe yourself.
Analyze — communicate findings honestly: good plots that lead to good understanding, defensible conclusions that lead to engineering decisions.

We’ll spend the most explicit time on Process and Simulate; Fetch and Analyze are woven through everything. The standards page lists what you’ll be able to do under each verb.

On paper (yes, actual paper), write a specification — 5 to 10 sentences — for this problem: a program that tells a student the fastest walking route between two buildings on campus. Your spec must state the inputs, the outputs, and at least three edge cases with what should happen in each.
Class opens with tables exchanging specs and hunting for the gaps.

title: First contact with coding
text:
Variables: giving numbers names
A variable is a name attached to a value, so you can use the value by its name:
g = 9.81        # gravitational acceleration, m/s^2
h = 3.0         # drop height, m


The text after a # is a code comment — a note for humans that Python ignores. Here, we described the physical meaning of the variables and included the units of the number.
Variable names can be simple or complex. Probably you will appreciate being able to write a simple, readable equation y=0.5*g*t**2 later in your code, but we also could have defined gravity_earth_surface = 9.81 and then used y=0.5*gravity_earth_surface*t**2 later on.






Tip



It is good practice to make the variable names descriptive such that you know what is going on in the equations involving those variables. Something like g in a mechanics-based program is probably fine because we are so used to seeing g in our mechanics equations. But if we had some code that involved gravity on earth and gravity on the moon (for some reason), it is better to write those as g_earth and g_moon instead of g_1 and g_2.


The = sign here does not mean “equals” in the algebra sense. It means “store the value under this name.” This structure conflicts with our experience in math class, for example:
count = count + 1
If we did algebra on this equation: subtract count from both sides, leaving 0=1… nonsense. But as an instruction, it will take the (current) value of count, add 1, and store the resulting value under the name count (thus replacing the old value stored under that name). This is perfectly acceptable practice, and indeed it is a common ingredient in code.

title: First contact with coding
section: A good habit to get into: predict, then run
text:
A good habit to get into: predict, then run
Here is a complete little program. Before you run it, write down what you expect it to display.






(Sure, you can run it without thinking. I’m not keeping track of what you are doing here… for the sake of your learning, I think you should think! Otherwise this is like the most boring game on the internet: click to see some text.)


** is, annoyingly, Python’s “raise to a power.” So x ** 0.5 is a square root. And * must always be written explicitly: 2h will give an error; you need 2 * h instead.
Some reading help: line 3 computes \(t = \sqrt{2h/g}\), the fall time of an object dropped from height \(h\), subject to gravity \(g\). So: \(2 \times 3 / 9.81 \approx 0.61\), and \(\sqrt{0.61} \approx 0.78\). That is: we predict this code should produce something near 0.78.
Now run it. It should match, unless you changed something in the code. Verification!

title: First contact with coding
text:
Errors are data
In the code above, change t = (2 * h / g) ** 0.5 to t = (2 * h_2 / g) ** 0.5, and run it again. You’ll get an angry red block ending in something like:
NameError: name 'h_2' is not defined
Two things to know about errors:
They are normal. Experts probably do make fewer errors, but they don’t make zero errors… and actually, I use errors as a way to write code faster: just write out a sloppy version of the code without expecting it to work, then: run, read and fix the error; run, read and fix the error; run, read and fix the error; and by then I’m probably done. Read the error messages, they usually describe the error and point to where it occurred in the code. Here: this is a NameError because we used a variable name that the program didn’t know.
They are the friendly failure mode. It is way more difficult to figure out why code runs successfully, but produces a wrong answer. Error messages are kind of nice because they tell you exactly what is wrong (maybe cryptically)!






Tip



Understanding error messages is a genuinely good use of an LLM: paste the code and the full error, and ask what’s wrong. Verify the explanation makes sense — don’t let the LLM do all your thinking for you!

title: Functions
text:
Getting an area from a radius, power from a resistance and current, distance traveled from velocity and time… these are calculations engineers do repeatedly. While we could write
… and then edit that code for every new calculation, we might instead write a function that takes current and resistance as inputs and produces power as an output. Any calculation we use over and over again is a good candidate for turning into a function. We’ll learn about functions in this lesson.

text:

title: Functions
text:
Anatomy of a function






This cell is live — feel free to edit it, break it, change the default gravity (Mars has \(g = 3.71\)).
What’s in here:

def is the syntax that starts a function definition.
fall_time is the function name (we choose it).
(h, g=9.81) are the function inputs, with g given a default value so callers can omit it. It can be included if you have need to change the parameter value.
Then we have an indented block that does the tasks we wrote the function for. Here, the function just does a bit of math.
The triple-quoted line is a docstring: the function’s specification, basically a comment that describes the function’s purpose. Technically optional, but a good idea.
return tells us the thing(s) that is (are) output once the function is done with its magic.



Defining a function does not mean the function runs. To actually get values from a function, we must call it: fall_time(3.0).
Calling it:
t1 = fall_time(3.0)          # drop from h = 3 m in Earth's gravity
t2 = fall_time(3.0, 1.62)    # same drop on the Moon
Before you run: should it take longer to fall when the gravity is lower? Verification!

title: Functions
section: The docstring is basically a specification
text:
The docstring is basically a specification
Look at fall_time(h, g=9.81) and its docstring — you know almost everything about the function from reading it: what goes in, with what units, what comes out, what’s assumed (from rest). A good problem specification practically writes the prompt and the docstring, but you can also ask for a good, detailed docstring in your prompt:

Write a Python function pressure_drop(L, D, Q) returning the pressure drop in Pa for laminar water flow through a smooth pipe of length L (m), diameter D (m), at flow rate Q (m³/s). Assume 20 °C water. Include a docstring stating the formula and its valid range.

title: Functions
text:
Check the function in isolation
Before a function enters any larger program: call it at least once with a case you can check by hand.
print(fall_time(3.0))   # hand estimate said ~0.78 — confirm before proceeding
Next week we’ll be calling functions inside loops, maybe 100 or 1000 times. Basically impossible to check all of them, but checking one or two… if they work out correctly, that is a good sign.

title: Functions
section: Local names: the function’s private scratchpad
text:
Local names: the function’s private scratchpad
It is probably easier to see this than understand an explanation. What do you predict will be printed in the following code?












NoteClick for the answer





5. The result inside double is local — it exists only while the function runs, in the function’s private workspace, and it is a different variable from the “outer” result, despite the shared name. This is a feature, not a hazard: it means you can use a function without knowing or caring what names it uses internally. Functions go inputs → output; the function interior is kept secret from the outside.

title: Functions
text:
Bring functions and AI together
The workflow that we’ll use for the rest of the semester: spec the function → prompt for it → annotate the body → hand-check it in isolation → use it. Notice that code production is the only thing delegated to AI, the other things are tasks that you handle, human engineer.






TipThink



The docstring says what the function should do. The annotation says what the function actually does. Verification is checking that those two are the same.



We’ll think about stopping distance for a car under braking. On paper write: the function definition line, a two-sentence docstring including assumptions and units, and one hand-checkable test case with its expected output (show the arithmetic). You don’t need to code the whole thing.
And here’s a description that you’ll base your work on: a car doesn’t stop the instant the driver decides to brake — there’s a reaction time first, maybe 1.5 s, during which the car just keeps cruising at speed \(v\). That chunk of distance is just speed times time, \(d_{\text{reaction}} = v \cdot t_{\text{reaction}}\). Then the brakes engage and the car decelerates from \(v\) to \(0\) at a roughly constant deceleration \(a\).
The kinematic equation is \(v_f^2 = v_0^2 - 2ad\). Since we’re solving for where the car finally stops (\(v_f = 0\)), it rearranges to \(d_{\text{braking}} = v^2 / (2a)\). Total stopping distance is the sum, \(d = d_{\text{reaction}} + d_{\text{braking}}\). One thing to check before you trust a number out of this: doubling \(v\) should more than double \(d\), since \(v\) shows up squared in the braking term.

title: Functions
text:
In-class work
We will implement the above function in Colab and then explore/understand some of the nuances.
Before each of these experiments, try to guess the behavior.






Caution



It is not necessarily true that your guess will match the actual behavior. Computers use a different logic than humans — e.g., they go through instructions sequentially and don’t have bigger-picture context. And programming languages have to make concessions — e.g. to square a number in Python we use
x=6
print(x**2)
It should be the case that x^2 is squaring… and it will be that way in MATLAB. But Python must have reserved the ^ character for something else, so we engineers get to use **.
The purpose of this section is to get you familiar with the structure of defining/calling functions and to caution you about some common missteps.


Before trying each, go to Runtime → Restart session. (This clears the function from the working memory.)

Call the function from below the function with numbers as inputs.
Call the function with variables as inputs. E.g. define v_start=50 and use v_start in the function call (instead of a plain number).

Convince yourself that the function variables are independent

Run the cell with the function in it, then run the next cell where you call the function.
Run the cell with the function in it, include the function call in the previous cell and run it.
If your function signature is stopping_distance(v_0,a,t_reaction=1.5), compare stopping_distance(1,10), stopping_distance(10,1), stopping_distance(a=10,v_0=1).
Try stopping_distance(25, reaction=2.0).
Try stopping_distance(reaction=2.0,25,10).







Important



Seeing this behavior yourself is much more instructive than me telling you about it! Programming is best learned actively!

Return multiple things
If you finish the above tasks early, here’s one more thing to try. We can return multiple outputs using
def some_fxn(x):
    ...
    return a,b
and then store those outputs with a similar structure in the call

Write a function that takes in the temperature in degrees Fahrenheit and returns the temperature in degrees Celsius and the temperature in Kelvin. Don’t use an LLM, you’ve got this!

title: For loops, and picking things out by index
text:
With NumPy arrays, we were able to take a bunch of wind speeds, throw them into a function we’d already written (with single wind speeds in mind), and get the corresponding power production back.
There’s another way we could have done this — a for loop. With a for loop, we go through the list of values one-by-one and perform the calculation. If that sounds less efficient, that’s because it is less efficient… so why would we ever want to use for? The answer is that arrays are great at one calculation, many numbers, but they are less capable when we need to consider many options and perform many calculations. In our design process, we wouldn’t have one turbine with a collection of wind speeds, we’d have five candidate turbines with a collection of wind speeds — which one is best? The for loop will help us with this calculation.

title: For loops, and picking things out by index
text:
Think First
Recall

What does speeds[power.argmax()] get you?
What does speeds[speeds >= 3] get you?

Look Ahead

Suppose you want the total day’s energy for five different rotor diameters. How many lines of code is that?
If a calculation gives you five answers, one per design, where do those five answers go? They aren’t the input array, and they aren’t a single number.

title: For loops, and picking things out by index
text:
A minimal for loop
A for loop runs the same indented block once for every item in a collection, in order:






How this structure works: it will assign D to the “zeroth” value in the diameters list, then run through the process in the indented block; then go back to the top of the block and reassign D to the “first” value in the diameters list, then run through the process in the indented block; then go back to the top of the block and reassign D …


Remember: Python indexes from 0!
crumbs: For loops, and picking things out by index

title: For loops, and picking things out by index
text:
“Wait, couldn’t NumPy do that?”
Here is something with a for loop






and here is something very similar without






The first one, with the for, is longer to write and longer to run — it is less efficient. So… why do we need for loops? I’ll try to say something general:

Arrays are good at holding data and then having math done on them. Very easy to cube every element in a list of 100 speeds in one line: speeds**3.
Loops are good at going through a collection of cases you are comparing. Five rotor diameters. Twelve tilt angles. Three modeling assumptions. Each pass through the loop produces a whole array’s worth of results (and then you’ve got to figure out what to do from there!).
crumbs: For loops, and picking things out by index

title: For loops, and picking things out by index
text:
Loop over designs, array inside
Let’s revisit the turbine calculation:






What happened on each pass through the for loop? The function turbine_power(good, D) handed back an array of seventeen powers. Then .sum() collapsed those seventeen numbers into one day’s energy. Then the loop moved on and did it again for the next diameter, then for the next diameter, and the next. In total we tested five diameters, each time using NumPy arrays+math to do the calculations necessary to get power.


Notice we didn’t change turbine_power. The power of functions, if you are thoughtful about how to build them, is that you can keep the same math inside them and just vary the inputs.
crumbs: For loops, and picking things out by index

title: For loops, and picking things out by index
text:
Where do the values go?
We’ve been relying on print a lot in this class, because we (humans) can see the answers. We also know we can save the values under a variable name. But now we are going to be producing massive amounts of data — large arrays for each test case… where do we store those values?

Option 1 — grow a list with append
Probably the most common method: create an empty list and append to it as you go through your for loop:






Three things happened here:

totals = [] makes an empty list before the loop — before, because anything created inside the loop would get wiped clean at the top of every pass.
totals.append(x) tacks x onto the end, so the list grows by one each time through.
np.array(...) converts the finished list into something we can do math on (recall that Python lists don’t cooperate with math).



Option 2 — pre-allocate and fill by index
Before the loop starts, build an array of the right size and fill it with placeholder values. Then each pass through the loop drops its answer into the slot that belongs to it. We know we’re testing multiple diameters, each needs a slot — and np.zeros(len(diameters)) gets that for us.






Same five numbers, by a different route. Three things happened here too:

totals = np.zeros(len(diameters)) builds the answer array before the loop, already the right size. len(diameters) is 5, so we get five zeros. Writing len(diameters) instead of just 5 means that when you change the list of designs, the answer array changes with it — you don’t have to remember to update a number in two places.
range(len(diameters)) is the sequence 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — every valid index of diameters. So this loop hands us positions rather than values, and we use the position twice.
Every time through the loop, we have set i to a particular value: 0, 1, 2, 3, then 4. Then totals[i] = ... drops one answer into slot i. We read diameters[i] and we write totals[i], both at the same index, on the same pass.

That third point explains why we do this: diameters[2] is the 100 m rotor and totals[2] is what the 100 m rotor made.






CautionZeros are a real number



If your loop skips a slot — you looped over range(4) when there were five designs, say — the last slot stays zero and there is no warning that you forgot about it.
The safer habit is to prefill with something that can’t be mistaken for an answer. np.full(len(diameters), np.nan) fills the array with nan — “not a number”. Any nan you fail to overwrite will poison every sum and max that it is involved in, loudly.





Option 3 — the list comprehension
There’s a third way that is difficult to comprehend but actually quite nice when you get used to it.






The whole loop — the empty container, the five passes, the collecting — has collapsed into that one bracketed expression towards the bottom. The trick to reading it is that the for is still in there, just moved. Read it back-to-front: for each D in diameters, evaluate turbine_power(good, D).sum(), and collect the results in a list. It’s the same as Option 1 but very succinct. The square brackets are doing the job that totals = [] and .append() were doing, which is why they’re brackets.


This is the most Pythonic of the three — that’s a real word people use, meaning roughly “written the way the language wants to be written.”
Option 3 is beautiful once it starts making sense! But it is dense and hard to read. Get comfortable with the other methods first.
crumbs: For loops, and picking things out by index

title: For loops, and picking things out by index
section: Indexing: getting one thing back out
text:
Indexing: getting one thing back out
Now that we’ve got a variable that contains all of our values, we can investigate them.








How to interpret the last line of this code:

totals.argmax() is 4 — the index of the largest energy.
diameters[4] is 120.0 — the design that lives at index 4.
So diameters[totals.argmax()] is “the diameter belonging to the best result.”

The two arrays are parallel: index 3 means the 110 m rotor in diameters and it means the 110 m rotor’s energy in totals, because we built them that way. Keeping parallel arrays lined up is important — if you mask one and forget to mask the other, index 3 no longer means the same design in both, a great way to confuse yourself or create incorrect results!






ImportantReminder: counting from zero



There is no totals[5] — you’ll get an IndexError.
Negative indices count from the right: totals[-1] is the last one, totals[-2] the second-to-last. This is useful: totals[-1] looks so much nicer than totals[len(totals)-1].



(1) Trace this by hand and write down the printed value:
total = 0
for x in [3, 7, 2, 9, 4]:
    if x > 4:
        total = total + x
print(total)
(2) Given these two parallel arrays:
tilt   = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40, 50])
output = np.array([277, 301, 315, 320, 315])
Write down what each of these gives you — the value, not a description:
output[1], output[-1], output.argmax(), tilt[output.argmax()], and len(tilt).
Then one sentence: if I dropped the first entry from output but not from tilt, what would tilt[output.argmax()] report, and would anything warn me?

title: Data in, data out — and honest plots
text:
Every number we’ve computed with so far, we typed into the program. The 24 hours of wind speed, the balloon’s \(k/m\), even the “sensor glitch” at −999 was manually typed-in. Real data doesn’t arrive that way. It arrives as a file — from a sensor, a colleague, a government agency — and it’s usually far too long to type.
This week we’re going to learn how to get numbers out of a program and into a file, and then how to get numbers from a file into a program. We’ll also talk about plotting, which we’ve been doing informally for a couple weeks but will be more detailed about now. Notably, we’ll talk about what good, honest plots look like, and how the default settings in our programming languages don’t really get us there. (And LLMs still do a bad job creating plots, in my opinion!)
crumbs: Data in, data out — and honest plots

title: Data in, data out — and honest plots
text:
Think First
Recall

In Colab, if you walk away for a couple hours, come back, and run a cell that uses a variable from earlier… what happens? Where did the variable go?
Week 4: diameters and totals were parallel arrays. What does that mean, and what breaks if they get out of line?

Look Ahead

If your program’s results need to be saved and sent to a colleague’s computer, how do we do that?
Can a plot be technically accurate and still be misleading?

title: Data in, data out — and honest plots
text:
Writing a file
Let’s start with results we already have. Here’s the design-speed sweep from week 4’s activity: eleven blade designs, one day’s energy for each. We’ll compute it exactly as before, and then add one line at the end.








This might not look very different from what we’ve been doing, but there is something extra happening in the background. I guess pyodide, the tool that is running code on this website, is saving a temporary file called “design_sweep.csv”, and then openining it and displaying the results. In Colab it is clearer that a file is created, and you can download it.
Within the np.savetxt function call:

"design_sweep.csv" is the file’s name. It is common to save arrays in a “comma-separated values” (csv) format.
np.column_stack([design_speeds, totals]) puts two parallel arrays together side by side as two columns. One row holds, for example, design_speeds[4] and totals[4].
delimiter="," puts a comma between the values in a row.
header="..." writes a first line naming the columns. This is your chance to give some details about the file contents — e.g., it might be a good idea to put the units in the names. A column called energy would leave the next reader guessing whether it’s kWh, MWh, or joules.
comments="" — see the margin.
fmt="%.1f" says “write each number with one digit after the decimal point.”



By default, savetxt puts # in front of the header line, marking it as a comment. NumPy is happy with that. Most other programs (Excel, pandas next week) are not, and they’ll think the first column is named # v_best_m_per_s. Setting comments="" turns that off.
Then print(open(...).read()) allows us to see the file on this webpage. In Colab you can just double-click the file to look at it (more on where it lives in a moment).

A file lives in a folder, and its full address is called its path. Something like /content/design_sweep.csv means “the file design_sweep.csv inside the folder content.” When we wrote just "design_sweep.csv" with no folder, Python put it in whatever folder it was currently working in.

title: Data in, data out — and honest plots
text:
Reading it back
Now the other direction. np.loadtxt reads a CSV of numbers into an array:






Two new things here. First, skiprows=1 tells loadtxt to skip the header line, because “v_best_m_per_s” is not a number, and loadtxt only reads numbers.
Second, data is a two-dimensional array — a grid, 11 rows by 2 columns, which is what data.shape reports. To get one value out of a grid we need two indices, row then column: data[4, 1] is row 4, column 1, which is the energy for the 10 m/s design. The colon means “all of them,” so data[:, 0] reads as “every row, column 0” — the whole design-speed column.


We are still counting from zero! Column 0 is the first column. Row 0 is the first row of numbers, since the header was skipped.
In practice we usually pull the columns apart right away and give them variable names, which gets us right back to the parallel arrays we know:
v_best = data[:, 0]
energy = data[:, 1]
print(v_best[energy.argmax()])
With this data now part of our program, we can do any sort of calculation we need to. Calculate the average, the max, the sum, etc.






Caution



Try deleting skiprows=1 from the cell above… you’ll get an error message.








Tip



Check out the file before computing anything: What are the columns, what are the units, does anything look strange?




loadtxt only reads numbers. A file with words or dates in it (a column like 2026-09-10, say) will cause problems.

text:
Plotting data
We’ve plotted some functions, e.g. \(C_p(v)\) and the falling ball. Plotting data works the same way, but might involve a couple different choices. Here are some Boulder temperatures, including a bad reading:






When we plot the data, the bad reading is obvious: it is the extreme outlier. A plot is a verification tool that looks at every row at once! So: plot the raw data before you process it.
A few standard choices when we plot data:

Markers, not lines, for measurements. "o" draws a dot at each data point with nothing in between. Our data collection is discrete, and so the representation of the data should be as well. (Theoretical equations or modeling equations can be solid lines because they are continuous.)
Labels with units. In many fields it is standard to report units you would not expect. For example, refrigerators are often measured in BTUs instead of the SI unit J. Don’t assume SI units — report the units in your plot!
A legend when there’s more than one thing. label= on each plot call, then plt.legend(). Or, if possible, add annotation arrows and label the data directly.

A plot can be an output file too. plt.savefig("boulder_sept.png", dpi=200), placed before plt.show(), writes the figure to Colab’s Files panel. You can download it and put it in a report.

text:
Honest plots
Here are the same six data points plotted twice: a motor’s efficiency, measured monthly.






On the left, the y-axis spans 0 to 100%, and the story is basically flat: a stable motor drifting up by half a percent. On the right, the axis spans 94.0 to 94.9%, the line is thick and red, the title sets misleading expectations, and the units have disappeared. The claimed story is that there has been a dramatic improvement. Neither plot contains a false number. I think the second one is still untruthful!






Caution



Try it: change the honest plot’s set_ylim(0, 100) to set_ylim(90, 100), then (94, 95).


Axis truncation is one way to make a misleading plot. Some other ways: a cherry-picked range (start the x-axis right after the bad quarter), missing units, two y-axes scaled to make unrelated things look correlated, 3D bars whose volumes exaggerate the differences.
As engineers, we should strive to produce plots that tell an accurate story. That includes being honest about bad data and uncertainty! We’ll also be on the receiving end of misleading plots and need to understand what the true story is so we can make good decisions.






TipThink



Is a truncated axis always dishonest? A half-percent drift might actually matter — maybe it is something wearing-in and we are monitoring to make sure it is following the typical pattern. In such a case, it may be a good (honest) idea to say what is happening: “note: y-axis spans 94–95% to show the drift over one month of use.”

text:
This week we are going to “fetch” data ourselves, instead of having a dataset given to us. Our first reading included the line:
We’ll know how to do this after today. We’ll learn what an API is, what the response looks like when it comes back (“JSON”, and Python reads it as a dictionary), and what to do when you don’t get a response.

title: Fetch: APIs and JSON
text:
Think First
Recall

Week 7: pandas let us grab a column by name (df["temp_C"]) instead of by position (AL2). Why was that such an improvement?
Week 6: before trusting any data file, what do you check?

Look Ahead

When the weather app on your phone shows today’s temperature, where does that number actually come from?
Suppose your program asks a server for data every 30 seconds for 20 minutes, and at minute 7 the Wi-Fi hiccups. What should your program do?

title: Fetch: APIs and JSON
text:
What an API is
An API (application programming interface) is, for our purposes, a web address that returns data instead of a web page. You send a question to a URL, and a computer somewhere sends back an answer.
Here’s one that gives the live position of the International Space Station. Click it on whatever device you’re reading this on:
https://api.wheretheiss.at/v1/satellites/25544
Refresh the page a few times and watch the numbers change… it’s moving fast!
That’s interesting, but we are probably more interested in using the answer. In Python:
import requests
r = requests.get("https://api.wheretheiss.at/v1/satellites/25544")
info = r.json()
print(info)
requests.get sends the request for information and .json() turns the reply into something Python can work with.



The code cells on this page run inside your browser, which isn’t set up for requests — so run in Colab. The cells below use a reply I saved earlier.

title: Fetch: APIs and JSON
text:
JSON, and the dictionary
Here’s what came back when I clicked that link on October 10 (lightly rearranged so it fits on the page):
{"name": "iss", "id": 25544,
 "latitude": 51.452776061797, "longitude": -116.29532419749,
 "altitude": 430.56388078893, "velocity": 27565.817344208,
 "visibility": "daylight", "timestamp": 1791654325,
 "units": "kilometers", ...}
This is JSON (“JavaScript Object Notation”, not only used with JavaScript), the format most APIs speak. Base Python has a dictionary that has a structure that looks like: "key": value. The above is a dictionary, and for example, name is a key, and iss is the associated value.
Dictionaries function similarly to a DataFrame in that we reference things by name, not by position:






Latitude 51.45° N, longitude 116.30° W. Paste 51.45, -116.30 into a map and the ISS was over the Canadian Rockies.
Now, is 27,566 a believable speed? The API says "units": "kilometers", so this is presumably km/h. Let’s check it against something we know: the ISS goes around the Earth about every 90 minutes. Its orbit is a circle of radius \(6371 + 431 \approx 6800\) km, so one lap is \(2\pi \times 6800 \approx 42{,}700\) km. At 27,566 km/h, that takes \(42{,}700 / 27{,}566 \approx 1.55\) hours, or about 93 minutes.

Never guess a key
What happens if we ask for a key that isn’t there? Try adding info["lat"] to the above cell. You should get KeyError: 'lat'.
Python won’t guess what you meant: the key has to match exactly, capitals and all. A good strategy: print the whole reply once, find the thing you want, and then write the path to it. Look first, then extract.


Nesting: dictionaries inside dictionaries
The ISS reply is simple: one level of keys. Most APIs aren’t. Here’s what a free weather service (Open-Meteo) sent back when I asked for the current conditions in Boulder:






weather["current"] is itself a dictionary, so we can index into it again: weather["current"]["temperature_2m"]. Read the path left to right, like directions: go to "current", then inside that go to "temperature_2m".
This reply also has something nice in it: the units travel with the data ("current_units"). Wind in km/h, not m/s or mph. And look at the time… 17:45 in "GMT". That’s not Boulder time. It was 11:45 in the morning here.

title: Fetch: APIs and JSON
section: When the question doesn’t get answered
text:
When the question doesn’t get answered
So far, every request worked. However: servers go down, Wi-Fi drops, free APIs get busy and tell you to slow down, and sometimes we just make a typo in the URL. Let’s see what failure actually looks like. Here’s the reply when I asked for a satellite number that doesn’t exist:
{"error": "satellite not found", "status": 404}
The server answered, but not with what we wanted: we got a JSON/dictionary with just two keys, "error" and "status". So if the next step in our code looks at info["latitude"] we’ll get a KeyError, and the program stops. If the Wi-Fi is down entirely, it’s worse: requests.get itself fails with a ConnectionError and never gets as far as a reply.
For one request in a notebook, a crash is fine: sigh and run the cell again. But maybe we’ve built a data logger that does an API request every 30 seconds for 20 minutes, and maybe we run it and step out for coffee. If there is a hiccup at minute 7, you’ll come back to a program that stopped 13 minutes ago. What we’d really like is for the program to say “that one didn’t work, skip it” and carry on.
That’s what try and except are for:






Python tries the indented block under try. If everything in it works, the except part is ignored. If anything in it fails, Python doesn’t crash. It jumps straight to the except block, runs that instead, and carries on with whatever comes next. err holds the error, so we can still see what went wrong.
In real fetching code, the try block would hold the request itself:
try:
    r = requests.get("https://api.wheretheiss.at/v1/satellites/25544", timeout=10)
    info = r.json()
    lat = info["latitude"]
except Exception as err:
    print("Skipped one reading:", repr(err))
(timeout=10 means “if there’s no answer in 10 seconds, give up.” Without it, a stuck request can wait a longggg time.)






Caution



try/except is powerful, and that makes it a little dangerous. It catches every error, including the ones that are your fault. Misspell a key inside a try, and the program will “skip” every reading without complaining. So keep the try block small (just where you need it), always print what was skipped, and count the skips at the end. Twenty requests with two skips is a hiccup, twenty requests with twenty skips is a bug.




There’s a third word in this family, raise, which lets your own code create an error on purpose: “this temperature is negative in kelvin, stop everything.” Useful when you write tools for other people to use.

title: Fetch: APIs and JSON
text:
In-class work
We’ll ask the ISS where it is a bunch of times, build a small dataset out of the answers, and use it to check the ISS’s speed a second way. Then we’ll point everything we learned at an API we’ve never seen.

One request. Fetch the ISS’s position with the three lines from the reading and print the whole reply. Pull out the latitude, longitude, altitude, and velocity. Where is it right now? Paste the coordinates into a map. Redo the 93-minute check with the altitude and velocity you got.
What time is it? The timestamp is a big number like 1791654325. That’s Unix time: the number of seconds since midnight UTC on January 1, 1970. (This is how most computers count time.) pd.to_datetime(info["timestamp"], unit="s") converts it. What time zone is it?
Ask several times, but patiently. We want to ask 10 times, 30 seconds apart, and keep the latitude, longitude, and time of each answer. The skeleton is below, with everything inside the loop removed except the waiting.
import time
import requests
import pandas as pd

url = "https://api.wheretheiss.at/v1/satellites/25544"
track = {"timestamp": [], "latitude": [], "longitude": []}

for k in range(10):

    # your code here

    time.sleep(30)          # wait 30 seconds before asking again

df = pd.DataFrame(track)
Before you write anything, talk with your partner: what is track? (Look at its curly braces.) Then write the body. Each pass through the loop should ask for the position, pull out the three values, add them to the three lists in track, and print the loop number k with either “ok” or the reason it was skipped. Think about what a skipped request should do, and where the try and except belong. One design question to settle before you run it: should you pull out all three values before appending any of them, or append each as you go? (What would happen to the three lists if "latitude" were missing from one reply?) When it’s working, it takes about 5 minutes, so keep the next step in mind while it runs.
While it runs, talk about time.sleep(30). This API allows about one request per second, and if it is busy it might allow even fewer. If a whole classroom did that in a loop it starts to look like an attack — we might get blocked!
Check your prediction. Look at df. How many degrees of longitude did the ISS cover in those ~5 minutes (first row to last)? (If you get something huge or negative, the track crossed the date line.) Compare with your bring-to-class prediction. They probably don’t match exactly. Can you think of why? (Hint: does the ISS actually fly along the equator? And what is the Earth doing underneath it?)
How fast did it go? Now we have positions and times, so we can measure the speed ourselves instead of reading it off the reply. Take the first row and last row of df. Between two nearby points on a sphere of radius \(R\), the distance traveled is
\[d = R\,\sqrt{(\Delta\varphi)^2 + (\cos\bar\varphi \cdot \Delta\lambda)^2}, \qquad v = \frac{d}{\Delta t}\]
where \(\varphi\) is latitude, \(\lambda\) is longitude, \(\Delta\) means (last − first), and \(\bar\varphi\) is the average of the two latitudes. The first term under the root is the north–south distance. The second is the east–west distance, with the \(\cos\bar\varphi\) there because a degree of longitude gets shorter as we move away from the equator. Both angles have to be in radians (after import numpy as np, np.radians converts and np.cos takes radians). Use \(R = 6371 + \text{altitude}\) in km, with the altitude from step 1, and get \(\Delta t\) in hours from the timestamps (which are in seconds). Compute \(v\) and compare it with the velocity from the API. Do they agree? If they’re off by a little, in which direction, and why?
Break it on purpose. Change the satellite number in url to 99999999, and run the loop for 3 requests (change range(10)). What does your program print? Look closely at which error it prints. Now take out the try/except (keep the code inside it) and run it again.

text:
A different API
The ISS API is one example. Now let’s use a different one that you’ve never seen, and use what we learned: print the reply, look at it, then write the path.
The US Geological Survey publishes a list of every earthquake it has detected on Earth, updated every minute. Here’s the past hour:
https://earthquake.usgs.gov/earthquakes/feed/v1.0/summary/all_hour.geojson

Look first. Fetch it. The whole reply is long, so don’t print all of it. Start with the keys at the top level (list(reply.keys())), then look at one piece. Where do the earthquakes live? What is each earthquake, and what’s the structure inside it?
Find the biggest. How many earthquakes were there in the past hour? (There are two places you could find that out; do they agree?) Which one had the largest magnitude, and where was it? Write the path to its magnitude and its place.
Where, and how deep? Each earthquake has "coordinates" with three numbers. Work out what they are, using the biggest earthquake’s place to check yourself. (Careful: this API doesn’t put them in the order the ISS one did!)
How long ago? An earthquake’s time is in the same Unix time as the ISS timestamp, but not in the same units. Figure out the units by finding when the biggest earthquake happened, then compare it against the reply’s generated time (in metadata) to find how many minutes ago it was. Does your answer sound plausible for a feed of “the past hour”?
Keep it going. Write a try/except loop that asks the USGS for the number of earthquakes in the past hour, five times, 10 seconds apart. (How often do you expect the answer to change? Is 10 seconds a sensible choice?)
